title: 40 Great Films for Christian Parents to Watch With Their Kids
summary: These excellent movies are enjoyable for families to watch together, but they’re also rich with values Christian parents can get behind.
content: In today’s glutted, morally compromised streaming-media environment, Christian families are right to worry about the countless options billed as “kid-friendly” but actually form kids in spiritually unhealthy ways. As a dad of four young kids, I know the struggle well. It’s impossible to keep up with the content conveyor belt of new film and TV options being marketed to kids. Christian parents need trusted curators who can reliably point us to entertainment that isn’t just “safe” for our kids to watch but is actively promoting laudable themes and (sometimes accidentally) modeling Christian virtue. This list is my attempt to help my fellow Christian parents in this struggle. The movies below are all G- or PG-rated and generally “safe for the whole family,” though parents should still consult online content guides to discern the appropriateness for their particular family. But the films I selected go beyond just safe . I commend them not only for what they don’t depict but for what they do. These movies are fun, well-made, and enjoyable for families to watch together ; they’re also rich with values Christian parents can get behind. These movies are rich with values Christian parents can get behind. I divided the list into two halves for different age groups: 20 films that might be better for your younger kids (9 and younger), and 20 films perhaps more appropriate for older kids (10 and older). If you have school-age kids, consider working your way through this list—making time not just to watch the movie together but also to discuss it afterward. Try to tease out the values and virtues the films celebrate. Cultivate in your kids a way of watching media wisely that might just become intuitive for them, with enough practice. To Watch with Younger Kids (9 and Younger) Beauty and the Beast (1991). For my money, this is the greatest of the great movies from the Disney animation heyday. The songs, the artistry, the themes of beauty, sacrifice, and love’s power to transform . . . the whole package is elegant and stately, with little of the “follow your heart” expressive individualism that compromises other Disney films of the era. Rated G. Cinderella (1950). Another all-time great Disney animated movie, the 1950 Cinderella is a gorgeous classic full of theological resonance. At a time when fairy tales and traditional romances are ridiculed or “modernized” in ways that blur moral lines, kids need the old stories where chivalric love is embraced and “happily ever after” endings aren’t pitched as problematic. Rated G. Coyote vs. Acme (2026). The newest release on this list, Coyote vs. Acme is one of the most enjoyable animated movies I’ve seen in years. Parents will laugh out loud at the satire and constant nostalgic callbacks, and kids will enjoy the vintage Looney Tunes physical humor. But more than just popcorn fun, this movie also celebrates unlikely friendship and perseverance in fighting for justice. Rated PG. David (2025). With animation as beautiful as any Disney or Pixar movie, this Angel Studios production about the biblical David blew my expectations away and landed on my top 10 list in 2025 . Biblically faithful and artistically excellent (the songs are catchy!), David has become a staple in our family’s rewatchable-movie diet. Rated PG. Despicable Me (2010). The Despicable Me franchise is one of my family’s favorites, and the first installment is rife with redemptive themes Christians can applaud. It’s the story of a hardened supervillain Gru (Steve Carell) who is morally transformed through the process of adopting three orphaned girls. Instead of the “good guy turns bad” trope that’s everywhere in pop culture, this is a “bad guy becomes better” story. Refreshing. Rated PG. Finding Nemo (2003). This is peak Pixar on both a storytelling and thematic level. The undersea adventure is visually stunning. But the film’s thematic explorations and insights for parenting are even richer. title: Why Christianity Explains Our Deepest Longings
summary: ‘Why Christianity Makes Sense’ offers a compelling argument that Christianity explains the condition of both the world and the human heart.
content: Throughout church history, God has raised up faithful voices to speak the gospel to each generation. The apostle Paul traveled through much of the known world, preaching in synagogues and public settings. In Athens, he used the questions the culture was asking as a platform from which to proclaim the gospel. Similarly, Augustine, Anselm, Blaise Pascal, C. S. Lewis, Tim Keller, and many others helped readers see Christianity’s coherence amid the questions and assumptions of their times. Through his online ministry, Truth Unites , Gavin Ortlund fills that sort of role in our cultural moment. In Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart , Ortlund offers an accessible defense of the faith for readers unsure whether Christianity can withstand serious examination. It’s also a useful tool for discipling believers bombarded with hard questions about Christianity on the internet. Ortlund’s goal is to show “why it makes sense to be a Christian” (xiii). Ortlund’s particular strength is that he recognizes our questions aren’t merely intellectual. They arise from deeper longings for meaning, purpose, and transcendence. Unknown God In Athens, Paul thoughtfully noticed an altar established “to the unknown god” (Acts 17:23). He didn’t mock them for it. Every generation builds an altar of its own. Augustine called it the restless heart; Lewis called it Sehnsucht , the longing that joy itself cannot satisfy. Keller called the traces it leaves behind clues . Ortlund has a name for it: “the ache.” Ortlund doesn’t begin with a technical exposition of the ache but by showing it’s the desire behind every altar to every unknown god. He asks, “Are you genuinely curious about what life means—why you’re here, and what it’s all for?” (xi). The ache is the restless longing for the transcendent that we can’t put into words. Just as hunger implies we live in a world where food is meant to fuel our bodies, so the desire for meaning points to the existence of something that will satisfy that desire. So many counterfeits promise to satisfy our desire for God. Many people have learned to deny any sense of longing for the divine or simply scroll past the question before it finishes loading in their minds. Just as hunger implies we live in a world where food is meant to fuel our bodies, so the desire for meaning points to the existence of something that will satisfy that desire. In a culture where the most shocking content on social media becomes boring, it’s worth drawing attention to Jesus’s radical claims. “He claimed to be the way, the truth, and the life,” notes Ortlund. “Muhammad taught the five pillars, Buddha spoke of enlightenment, Confucius pointed to the Way, but Jesus pointed to himself as the answer. In fact, Jesus claimed to be God” (104). The claim is preposterous, unless it’s true. So Ortlund asks his readers to put on their thinking caps: “What if God is real, and Jesus is this God, showing up in history to reveal himself to us? Why not? Is it really all that much crazier than the alternatives?” (104). It’s not. And more importantly, the solution Jesus offers is the most complete answer to the ache. This message deserves to be proclaimed in public. In the Marketplace When Paul was in Athens, he “reasoned . . . in the marketplace” (Acts 17:17), the agora, which is where ideas were exchanged. Our modern agora is increasingly virtual, less of a town square and more like the comment section of a microvlog. Ortlund has excelled in this space, making hard things plain in his videos without making them small. His talent for public communication comes through in this book. For example, Ortlund tackles divine hiddenness: Have you ever wondered why, if God is indeed real, his existence isn’t completely obvious? Why are religious matters so ambiguous ? Wouldn’t a loving God want to make things clear to us? (176) It’s an intuitive argument that undermines the sense that the ache is a longing
author: Thomas West

title: Using Exercise to Help Us Through the Dark Times (with Lindsey Bomgren)
summary: Fitness can be a vain, selfie-driven world. Lindsey Bomgren, founder of Nourish Move Love, shares how she found her calling there: helping women get ‘strong for their tasks’ through difficult seasons and circumstances.
content: In this episode of Your Corner of the World , Dan Doriani and Mark Vroegop talk with Lindsey Bomgren, founder of Nourish Move Love , a Minneapolis-based fitness business that has spent 11 years helping women get strong at home. A former college athlete and a mother of three, Lindsey built one of the internet’s top-ranked postpartum workout programs, and she wrestled with God for years over whether a career in fitness could serve anyone at all. Lindsey explains why Christians shouldn’t treat their bodies as an afterthought, drawing on Proverbs 31 (“Her arms are strong for her tasks,” NIV), Paul’s words on physical training and godliness, and the parable of the talents. She tells the story behind the name Nourish Move Love, opens up about a dark postpartum season that gave her new empathy for struggling women, and offers practical encouragement for beginners: Have a plan, remember that 10 minutes is better than zero, and trade appearance-based goals for progress-based ones. She also describes the long grind of building a business by giving her content away, and the burnout that led her to rethink it. Resources Mentioned: Blue Ocean Strategy by W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne The Body Teaches the Soul by Justin Whitmel Earley Habits of the Household by Justin Whitmel Earley
author: Dan Doriani, Mark Vroegop, Lindsey Bomgren

title: Small-Church Elders, Here’s How to Give Your Pastor a Sabbatical
summary: Our church has 74 members and two lay elders. Here’s how we raised up five men to preach seven expository sermons and give our pastor a summer sabbatical.
content: “He should have had a sabbatical six years ago,” my fellow elder said. “I know,” I said. “We know he needs it, but how are we going to do this? We have full-time jobs and young families.” “Well, the cattle on thousand hills are the Lord’s. Let’s ask him to provide it.” I nodded in agreement, but honestly, cattle felt like less of an ask for our church. Our church consists of 74 members. We have one full-time pastor and two lay elders. And yet, exactly two years after that initial elders’ meeting, we managed to give our pastor a much-needed, six-week summer sabbatical. Five male members of our church delivered seven expository and Christ-exalting sermons. God was glorified, our pastor rested, and our church loved it. We preached through an entire book of the Bible (Habakkuk). We preached a doctrinal sermon from our confession of faith (on baptism and Communion). Two men preached for the first time. The men ranged from age 20 to 46, and I was the seasoned preacher with 25 sermons under my belt. So how did we pull this off? 1. We prayed. We knew we couldn’t do this. Only God could. This reality framed our prayers over the next two years. God was glorified, our pastor rested, and our church loved it. We came to realize that just as the Sabbath was a gift from God to man (Mark 2:27), so a sabbatical is a gift from God to a pastor. As lay elders, we were called to take steps of faith to this end while relying on the Holy Spirit’s leading and enablement. Just as Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath (Matt. 12:8), so too is he Lord of a sabbatical. As we began to make plans, we prayed that we’d hold them with an open hand and continually lay them at the feet of Jesus. We borrowed words from Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 20:12) for our prayer in this season: “Lord, we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” 2. We planned backward. We began by identifying the ideal time of year for the sabbatical. We landed on July and August, since that’s when church programming is minimal and vacations are in vogue among our congregation. This decision indirectly led us to the length of sabbatical we felt could responsibly plan for: six weeks. From there, we planned backward. The first Sunday we discussed was the Sunday our pastor would return. How did we want our brother and his wife to reintegrate into the church? We decided we wanted him to feel the warmth of our church’s love in his homecoming without being distracted by sermon preparation. So we chose to begin and end his sabbatical on Fridays. This meant our pastor had a workweek before leaving, so he could help with administrative functions. And by returning from the sabbatical on a Friday, he’d be able to join us for an elder meeting to get updates on members prior to attending church two days later. Preaching could wait another week. We created a two-year timeline that included all of the specific events and developments we thought could be feasible with the Lord’s help. This timeline helped us to answer several looming questions: Should we start the sabbatical by sending our pastor somewhere to create physical and emotional separation between him and our congregation? We agreed we should. We also felt this was an opportunity to invite our church to be generous and to tangibly show their love to our pastor of 12 years and his wife by paying for this trip. How many of our male members would be willing to assist with the preaching? We estimated three to four. How and when would we get them trained? This was the hardest question to answer but also the most rewarding part of this process. 3. We created a brotherhood. We realized our biggest hurdle would be recruiting and training men to aid in the preaching. To address the issue, we settled on offering a six-week preaching cohort during the summer prior to the sabbatical. title: Where Our Criminal Justice System Breaks Down (with Matt Martens)
summary: Matt Martens joins Collin Hansen to discuss justice, citizenship, and Christian responsibility.
content: When you really want to dive into the details of big questions about public policy—how we can live better together—you run into two problems: The experts and other stakeholders don’t want to consider Christian arguments, and Christians don’t want to engage in the details. That combination of a Christian argument from a legal expert was rare when Matt Martens’s book Reforming Criminal Justice: A Christian Proposal came out in 2023 from Crossway. And it’s still rare today. Matt is a trial lawyer and partner at an international law firm in Washington, DC. He and his wife are members at Capitol Hill Baptist Church, and they have two sons and a daughter. I read this book when it came out, and it’s stuck with me. Just the other day, I was thinking about the book when talking to one of my pastors, who was preparing to preach from 1 Peter on justice and obeying authorities. I thought about how I’d want to see the criminal justice system reformed if there were a good shot I’d be either a victim or criminal defendant. Isn’t that the law summed up in loving our neighbors as ourselves? From the death penalty to AI to the decline of violent crime—Matt and I covered a great deal. In This Episode 00:00 – Why poor defendants often lack adequate legal representation 02:00 – The biggest misconception about the American criminal justice system 03:32 – The criminal justice reform Matt would prioritize first 07:21 – DNA evidence, wrongful convictions, and the fallibility of the system 13:26 – Why Matt opposes the death penalty as currently practiced 19:43 – Why preaching the gospel doesn’t eliminate our responsibility to pursue public justice 22:23 – Why Christians should serve on juries 27:38 – What decades as a lawyer taught Matt about how justice actually works 39:56 – Raymond Flanks: faith after nearly 39 years of wrongful imprisonment 46:26 – How AI could transform legal work and expand access to justice Resources Mentioned: Reforming Criminal Justice by Matthew T. title: The Cumulative Effect of Thousands of Family Bible Times
summary: When your kids are inattentive or disruptive, don’t be overly discouraged. If the milk spills, if a fight erupts, all is not lost.
content: The alarm goes off, and another busy day begins. Getting kids up and ready for school, meal prep, work, after-school activities. Before you know it, the day is racing to its close. And you’re exhausted again. As Christian parents, we want our lives to count for Christ. We sincerely want our children to live their lives for Christ too. We want them to be changed by the same amazing grace that has transformed us. But how does this happen? How can we find the time and energy to effectively disciple our kids? Where will we find the creativity and passion to teach them what matters most? If you’re discouraged by your limited time and ability to shepherd your children, consider the cumulative effects of thousands of family Bible readings over the course of many years. Think Small What if a brief Bible reading today, a couple more later this week, and a few more next week eventually became a pattern, a deeply rooted habit for your family? Small investments of time and intentionality can make a big difference over a couple decades. Small investments of time and intentionality can make a big difference over the span of a couple decades. Years ago, Trevin Wax wrote an article titled “ 1000 Sermons Will Change Your Life .” What he says to pastors about preaching also applies to parents who lead their kids in family Bible reading: Pastors, don’t underestimate the cumulative effect of your preaching. You are not dumping information into brains. You are forming the habits of your people, teaching them how to read and understand and apply the Bible for themselves. Similarly in family life, our discipleship has cumulative effects that may not come to fruition for years. As parents, we’re in this for the long haul. If your children live in your home from birth to age 18, that’s 6,570 days. If you read the Bible together on average every third day, that’s 2,190 Bible readings over the course of your sons’ and daughters’ childhood and teenage years. Keep that big picture in mind when you feel defeated after a couple days on the go, when those family discipleship moments have eluded you. Think of Timothy, who was acquainted with the sacred writings from childhood because of his mother’s and grandmother’s faithful witness (2 Tim. 1:5; 3:14–15). May we be influential parents like them, who little by little and day by day pass on our life of faith to the next generation. Be Consistent, Establish a Habit With the long view in mind, think small in terms of your goals for this week, month, or year. Aim for consistency, for establishing a habit that you can pray will take root in your kids’ lives. Joe Carter recently shared the results of a sociological study of how faith moves across generations. He summarized the findings: The behaviors that most strongly predict lasting faith are active and verbal: praying together as a family, saying grace, embedding faith in the rhythm of the week rather than reserving it for Sunday, and, above all, talking about it. Children raised in homes where faith was discussed at least several times a week were more than twice as likely to attend church, pray daily, and rate religion as very important in young adulthood. The simplest way to put this truth into practice in your home is by creating a rhythm of opening the Bible regularly, reading some verses, and discussing them. You may never have a sense that one particular devotional was transformative. But keep at it. When your kids are inattentive or disruptive, don’t be overly discouraged. If the milk spills, if a fight erupts, all is not lost. Resist the temptation to quit. Come back to the reading the next day, or the day after that. Keep finding times to open the Bible with your family. Let the Word Do the Heavy Lifting Another deterrent that may get in the way of family discipleship is “the intimidation factor.” If you feel ill-equipped to teach the Bible to your kids, you may be inclined to leave that task to Sunday school teachers and youth pastors. title: Would God Ever Say, ‘I Will Save You No More’?
summary: Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our repentance, as important as that is. Our hope ultimately rests on the compassion of our God.
content: Parents know that not every “I’m sorry” is the same. Sometimes “I’m sorry” means “I’m sorry I got caught” or “I’m sorry I’m facing the consequences.” Yet sometimes it means “I was wrong. Will you forgive me?” Parents also don’t respond to every apology the same way. Sometimes we immediately embrace our child. Other times we slow the conversation down. We ask questions. We press a little deeper, because we don’t just want to hear the words “I’m sorry.” We want those words to reflect a changed heart. In Judges 10, we encounter shocking words. The Lord says, “I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress” (vv. 13–14). Would God ever speak words like that to us ? Like a good parent, God knows there are different kinds of “I’m sorry,” and he’s not satisfied with words alone. He sometimes speaks to his people in surprising ways because he’s after our hearts. Lord’s Holy Rebuke The book of Judges follows a familiar pattern. Israel sins. The Lord gives them over to their enemies. They cry out. Then the Lord raises up a deliverer (e.g., 2:10–16). But that pattern isn’t merely a repeating cycle—it’s a downward spiral. Like a good parent, God knows there are different kinds of ‘I’m sorry,’ and he’s not satisfied with words alone. By Judges 10, Israel has descended deeper into idolatry than ever before. No longer content to run after the gods of the Canaanites, they’ve collected gods from every surrounding nation. Consequently, their existence hangs in the balance as their enemies move into Israel’s heartland. Yet as Israel’s sin and misery reaches a new low, their confession reaches a new height. For the first time in Judges, Israel confesses their sin (v. 10). But apparently, the Lord has heard this speech before . He knows when “I’m sorry” is little more than words. So instead of raising up another deliverer, he reminds Israel of his repeated acts of salvation (vv. 11–12). Then comes the striking statement: “I will save you no more” (v. 13). Those words should unsettle us. They certainly would’ve unsettled Israel. God’s words expose their dangerous presumption. For generations, Israel assumed the pattern would continue. They thought they could repeatedly forsake the Lord and simply return to him whenever life became unbearable. But not this time. The Lord’s rebuke shatters their assumption. You chose your gods. Cry out to them. Let them save you. The Lord exposes both their idols’ emptiness and their hearts’ audacity. Their gods cannot save them. And the Lord won’t be treated as an emergency deliverer while his people give themselves to other gods. Moreover, the Lord’s rebuke isn’t just for Israel. It’s meant to confront us today. These words were written for our instruction (1 Cor. 10:11). We also shouldn’t assume we can cling to our idols, live in our sin, ignore God’s commands, and then simply cry out to him when life falls apart. God isn’t manipulated by empty words. His rebuke exposes our idols and confronts our presumption. He calls us to repentance. Lord’s Compassion When the Lord rebukes Israel, they finally move beyond mere words to genuine repentance. They put away the foreign gods and serve the Lord (v. 16). As soon as they do, we read, “[The Lord] became impatient over the misery of Israel.” Or we might translate it, “He could bear Israel’s suffering no longer” (v. 16, JB). One of the most shocking verses in Judges is followed by one of its most beautiful. The God who rightly opposes sin is also moved by his people’s suffering. The God who says “I will save you no more” is the same God who only bears his people’s misery for so long. Certainly, this passage calls for genuine repentance. Yet when it explains God’s response, it doesn’t point us first to Israel’s motivation but to God’s . It doesn’t say, “Israel’s heart was finally sincere.” It says, “[The LORD] became impatient over the misery of Israel.” Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our re

title: When You Need a Christmas Miracle
summary: We won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all.
content: Read Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. (Isa. 7:14) Reflect If you watch even a few holiday movies this year, you’ll encounter the trope of the “Christmas miracle.” The festive season apparently has the magical ability to bring soulmates together, rescue floundering family businesses, and heal incurable diseases. The impossible becomes possible when December 25 rolls around. The nation of Judah in Isaiah’s day was in dire need of a miracle. They were in a centuries-long cycle of sin and rebellion against God. The northern kingdom of Israel had joined forces with Syria, and together they threatened to attack. Judah’s evil king, Ahaz, wouldn’t submit to God. What hope did they have? The impossible becomes possible when December 25 rolls around. Despite Ahaz’s hard-heartedness, God shows grace by making a promise: “The Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isa. 7:14). Later, in Matthew’s Gospel, we learn that “Immanuel” means “God with us” (Matt. 1:23). A spark of light appears in Judah’s dark future. But it didn’t seem like it could happen. A virgin bearing a son? Impossible. God dwelling among sinful people? Impossible. Yet this is what we celebrate at Christmas. Matthew recounts Jesus’s birth and tells us that “all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet” (v. 22)—Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of God’s promise through Isaiah. God did the impossible. What seems impossible to you this Christmas? You may have a list of tasks, commitments, and events so long that you can’t possibly get it all done—let alone with a sense of peace, contentment, or even sanity. You may be facing family conflict, and you don’t know how to begin healing the divides. You may be grieving, and the prospect of finding any holiday joy seems remote. God doesn’t promise to do everything that seems impossible. On Christmas morning, we won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all. Impossible as it once seemed, God himself “came into the world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15). He’s with us now by his Spirit, and one day he’ll return to make a new world and dwell with us physically and eternally. We won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all. So this Advent season, look to your God who does the impossible. Pray earnestly for peace and rest, for healing, for reconciliation, for joy. But remember he has already given us what we need. He’s redefined what’s impossible: “Neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38–39). It’s impossible that he’ll abandon us. Because God is steadfastly with us, we can face what seems insurmountable this Christmas. Our weaknesses and sins will not hinder God’s determination to save and dwell among his people. He is God with us, now and forever, as the apostle John sees in his vision of the future: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Rev. 21:3). Respond What impossible situation are you facing this Christmas? Spend time praying about that today. Consider what we learn about the Lord from these verses and how that changes the way you think about your struggles or fears. What difference does it make that God is with you?
author: Cassie Achermann

title: What Roman History Can (and Can’t) Explain About Christianity
summary: ‘Rome’s Age of Revolution’ is a tightly argued book that makes a number of important connections between the Greco-Roman world and the formation of the early church.
content: Of all the paradoxes and tensions in Rome’s Age of Revolution , none is so striking as the contrast between the book and its dustcover. That’s not the fault of the author, Tim Whitmarsh, currently regius professor of Greek at the University of Cambridge. Nor is it unheard of for publishers to exaggerate the novelty, originality, controversy, or even scandal of a particular thesis, especially when promoting scholarly arguments to a wider audience. But it jars nonetheless. And it has the unfortunate effect of creating undeliverable expectations, which turn a clear, brief, well-written, thoughtful, and perfectly reasonable book into a slight disappointment. “This remarkable book redefines early Christianity,” proclaims the first endorsement on the back cover. “Dazzling. This thrilling and elegantly written book will change how you see Rome, and Christianity, for ever,” says the next. The breathlessness continues. Harry Sidebottom says it “makes us rethink everything we know about the rise of Christianity.” Candida Moss commends it for “for ever changing how we think about the entanglement of empire, culture and early Christianity.” The inside jacket has fewer references to “everything” and “for ever,” but praise for the book’s originality continues: “Offers a whole new way to view Christians as an integrated part of the whole, multifaceted ancient Mediterranean world.” And so forth. There’s nothing wrong with rave reviews and ringing endorsements, of course. The problem in this case is that they lead the reader to anticipate a fresh, bold, provocative, and potentially explosive new argument, which is exactly what Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire, and the Making of Christianity doesn’t provide. What it offers instead is a measured, straightforward, run-of-the-mill presentation of a widely accepted view—that Christianity “was decisively and fundamentally shaped by the culture that incubated it” (228), both Greek and Roman, and “could not have come into being in anything like the form we know it without the revolutionary impact of Augustus’ political reforms” (230)—to a nonspecialist audience. Little in here is new, or claims to be. Plenty of it is found embryonically in Eusebius, Chrysostom, Thomas Aquinas, and John Calvin, to say nothing of F. F. Bruce or N. T. Wright. Integration and Conflict Whitmarsh revels in nuance, not controversy. “From one perspective, Christianity changed everything. From another, it reflected the world around it” (xxiv). It would be simplistic, for example, to frame an argument in terms of Greco-Roman cultural influence on early Christianity, because influence flows both ways. It would be equally simplistic to point out all the ways in which the ante-Nicene church aped and adapted imperial Rome without noting the ways in which they had nothing to do with each other: “There was very little that was Augustan about, for example, the Eucharist” (231). Similarly, although “most Christians were fully integrated into Roman society, and no more or less harassed than anyone else” (184), and although many stories of Christian martyrdom were stylized, embellished, or even invented, there’s no doubt that emperors like Decius and Diocletian pursued “systematic, pan-imperial action” and “vindictively anti-Christian policies” (186) and that “Christian zealots were certainly executed” (204). His analogy is apt: Although we know that the representation of cowboys and Indians in a western movie is usually a cinematic distortion, it would be a mistake to assume on that basis that conflict between settlers and indigenous peoples in North America in the nineteenth century was entirely the invention of Hollywood. (203–4) The book is at its best in parts 1 and 2, when describing the endlessly fascinating world of the late Roman republic and early Roman empire, and the ways in which it made Christianity’s message comprehensible and its expansion possible. title: Young Adults Are Hungry. Here Are 3 Ways to Feed Them.
summary: Gen Z’s hunger for food, people, and the Word gives the church a magnificent opportunity in this moment.
content: When we opened the century-old church doors on the corner of Whaley Street and Wayne Street, we figured we’d have about 50 folks step through them that night. It was a Bible class for Gen Z, after all. How many Gen Zers actually want to learn about the Bible? Apparently, more than 50. We had to scramble for more chairs. It quickly became obvious that this generation—my generation—is hungry for the Bible, and we’ll starve if we don’t get fed. How are you feeding the hungry young adults in your context? My church has learned key lessons about feeding college students and young adults. These aren’t novel, but I hope they can help your people as much as they’ve helped ours. 1. Food (Like, Actual Food) I was sitting across from a leader at a major university recently and asked him how we could influence the students on that campus. He looked at me and said the plainest thing: “Food wins.” To win the heart of a man, you go through the stomach. If you want to feed people the gospel, consider first feeding them a sandwich. This is why my brother (“Chef Chunk” as they call him) has been serving an incredible amount of pancake batter out of a four-foot plastic storage container, complete with chocolate chips, blueberries, and a few other cheap toppings. We start pancake-flipping before 7 p.m. and don’t stop until we start class at 8:03 p.m., to keep up with the demand. Apparently breakfast for dinner is a fan favorite. Eating meals with others is one of the greatest indicators of personal well-being—the more we eat with our families (whether spiritual or biological), the more likely we are to be satisfied with our lives and filled with love, joy, and peace. Yet we’re eating fewer meals together than ever. What if the church was one of the great combatants of this damaging trend? 2. Friends (Like, Actual Friends) Speaking of loneliness, our culture is increasingly lacking “third spaces” where lonely people can find and build community. Robert Putnam described and predicted this decades ago in Bowling Alone —but these days we don’t just bowl alone. We shop alone, eat alone, entertain alone. We even tend to date or do friendship “alone,” as in virtually rather than in person. What few third spaces remain—the gym, sports environments, coffee shops—aren’t ideal for making meaningful connections. In gyms, we have our headphones on; at sports games, the music is so loud you get hoarse when you speak; and coffee shops are great but usually filled with headphones-on, screened-off people (and $7 lattes). Fresh-out-of-college Jimmy has nowhere to meet potential-best-friend Johnny or potential-love-of-his-life Jessica. That leaves Jimmy feeling hopeless in one of the most foundational needs of life: relationships. Our culture is increasingly lacking ‘third spaces’ where lonely people can find and build community. Yet this is a hole best filled by the new humanity God created called the church. Amid a growing cultural hunger for embodied friendships, maybe one of the major ways our church can “seek the welfare” of our cities (Jer. 29:7) is to build environments where a wide variety of folks can congregate. Maybe that looks like creating spaces for line-dancing, pick-up basketball, or weekly pickleball nights. But I have a hunch that one of the most interesting third spaces we can create might not need to be about entertainment. 3. Knowledge (Like, Spiritual Knowledge) “Do you know what Christmas is about?” “Um—not sure. What do you mean?” “Like, do you know the story behind it?” “Hmm. I feel like it’s about a guy . . .” “YES! Do you know his name?” “Mmm. Nah man.” “Jesus. His name is Jesus.” This is a real conversation I had with an average high school student in the South, the heart of the so-called Bible Belt. I could tell you of dozens of other conversations just like it. Here’s the truth: The Bible is the most interesting story in the world, and no one knows it anymore. Christians have a tragic habit of making this story far less interesting tha

title: The Festive Attire We Really Need
summary: Even in our finest clothes we can still be dirty on the inside. Advent reminds us that Jesus dresses us in his righteousness.
content: Read He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD. Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years. (Mal. 3:3–4) Reflect My grandmother always made going to church a special event. She helped me pick the right dress, made sure my shoes were shiny and clean, and withstood burns from the curling iron to perfect my hairdo. I know church attire can vary. But I still get dressed up for corporate worship because, no matter how cliché it sounds, I want to wear my Sunday best for Jesus. Yet even in our finest clothes, we can still be dirty on the inside. Hidden sins are, after all, hidden. We can sing hymns at max volume, forgetting the way we treated our coworkers last week. We can kneel in prayer, easily dismissing what we posted on the internet earlier that morning. We can take the bread and wine even if we lost it with our kids in the car. People at church only see what’s on the outside, but God looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). And unless we come clean, we can’t come into his presence at all. Even in our finest clothes, we can still be dirty on the inside. Purity in God’s presence is a major theme in Scripture. In Leviticus, we learn how Israel was to distinguish between the clean and unclean. These categories extended to foods and animals. Even people could be defiled by disease or by touching unclean things such as a dead body. The temple was off-limits for the unclean. Only ritual washings and animal sacrifices made reentry into God’s presence achievable. But even this wasn’t permanent—for the blood of bulls and goats couldn’t fully atone for sin (Heb. 10:4). Like Israel, we dare not present ourselves before God in our sinful condition. As the psalmist asks, “Who shall stand in [God’s] holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Ps. 24:3–4). While soap and water might wash our filthy hands, what can purify our sin-stained hearts? In today’s verses, the prophet Malachi announced the coming of One who would refine his people as gold and silver. Later, the author of Hebrews clarified the refiner’s identity: If the blood of goats and bulls . . . sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God. (Heb. 9:13–14) During Advent, we remember that Jesus is the great Refiner. He came to shed his purifying blood to cover our sins and forgive us. Then, like a refiner who heats metal to remove impurities, the Lord sanctifies us so that on judgment day we’ll be an unblemished offering to God. On that day, because of Jesus, we’ll wear white robes of righteousness (Rev. 6:11). Grandma made sure I looked pretty for church, but I wasn’t truly clean. Jesus, the great Purifier of sinners, is the only One who can wash away every stain and remove every impurity. When he dresses us in white robes, we’ll enter God’s presence because we’ll be clean—not just on the outside but on the inside too. Respond Sometimes the Lord refines us through trials and difficult circumstances. How have you experienced his refining process this year? Write a prayer thanking God for Christ who cleanses, purifies, and refines us so we’ll one day be holy and acceptable in his presence.
author: Sharonda Cooper

title: Don’t Be Afraid of the Alien Question
summary: ‘Faith in Space’ shows that many Americans throughout history have already taken the question of extraterrestrial life seriously, but they’ve done so from outside an orthodox Christian framework.
content: Have you ever wondered whether other worlds exist, and, if they do, whether they’re filled with intelligent life? If so, you’ve tapped into a deeply human instinct. Americans have long looked up at the night sky and asked that question. For Christians, though, the answers can feel unnerving. We already believe in nonhuman intelligence. We call them angels and demons. But aliens would be something else—material, embodied, literally otherworldly . In 2016, NASA started a conversation among religious scholars at the Center of Theological Inquiry in Princeton about what the existence of extraterrestrial life would mean for religion. Paul Gutjahr, Ruth N. Halls professor of English at Indiana University, has been wrestling with that question for years. Faith in Space: American Religious Belief in Extraterrestrial Life is his considered answer. He thinks we need to look back at existing “extraterrestrial cosmologies” in American religions rather than merely pondering future possibilities (7). Faith in Space is ultimately a history of what happens when religious communities take extraterrestrial life seriously. Many minority religions have, and it has shaped their cosmology and even their soteriology. But for many evangelical Christians, Gutjahr’s history raises a more uncomfortable question: What happens when we don’t take seriously the possibility of extraterrestrial life? Alien Religion Early Americans didn’t need much help imagining inhabited worlds. According to Gutjahr, many Americans “believed there to be life elsewhere in the universe” (19). By the end of the 19th century, “every stratum of American society had been exposed” to this belief (43). For example, Emanuel Swedenborg taught that the universe is populated with humans bearing God’s image and claimed to have conversed with them. His American followers never numbered more than a few thousand, and yet his ideas traveled across the young nation; Helen Keller held them, as did John Chapman (a.k.a. Johnny Appleseed). What happens when we don’t take seriously the possibility of extraterrestrial life? Andrew Jackson Davis, the father of American Spiritualism, was similarly inspired, convinced that “if life is to be found on other planets, it is human life.” He arranged extraterrestrial humans in “a progression of degrees that move from less to more spiritual” (64). Then Joseph Smith took things further. Latter-day Saints (Mormons) took an “aggressive extraterrestrial cosmological stance,” linking all worlds under one governing structure (79). God created many inhabited worlds arranged in “a hierarchy where some worlds rule over others” (89). Among these many worlds, Earth holds the least desirable title of “the most wicked, and thus most in need of a savior” (86). God himself is an enfleshed exalted man dwelling on a planet near the star Kolob. I’d add that the Salt Lake Temple bears the Big Dipper, and early Latter-day Saint temple iconography is thick with suns, moons, and stars. Next came the founder of Seventh-day Adventism, Ellen G. White. Where William Miller’s followers read comets and meteor showers as signs of Christ’s return, White gave Seventh-day Adventists “a far more complex understanding of their relationship with the stars” (124). Ours “was the only wicked world” (125). White distinguished strongly between the righteous and unrighteous worlds, and put Earth on the wrong side of that distinction. By the 20th century, the heavens were packed and theories about the heavens were part of salvation. Then comes Helena Blavatsky (Theosophy), L. Ron Hubbard (Scientology), Wallace Fard Muhammad and Louis Farrakhan (Nation of Islam), Malachi Z. York (Nuwaubian Nation), Ashtar Command, and Heaven’s Gate. All these figures or groups saw extraterrestrial life as part of the human story, whether for our good or our ill, or both. While the subtitle promises to cover American religions broadly, Gutjahr sets aside Catholics, Jews, and native traditions. The only “Protestants” h

title: Fulani Militants Kill 14 Christians in Plateau State, Nigeria
summary: At least 14 Christians have been killed in fresh attacks across four local government areas of Plateau state, Nigeria, days after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu appealed for forgiveness over his failure
content: At least 14 Christians have been killed in fresh attacks across four local government areas of Plateau state, Nigeria, days after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu appealed for forgiveness over his failure to visit violence-affected communities during an earlier trip to the state and promised to rebuild destroyed communities and return internally displaced persons (IDPs) to their ancestral homes. The killings occurred between Sunday, Nov. 15, and Monday, Nov. 16, in Mangu, Riyom, Barkin Ladi and Bokkos local government areas, according to community sources and local security groups. Armed attackers reportedly targeted rural settlements and ambushed residents traveling between communities. The latest violence followed Tinubu’s visit to Jos on Saturday, Nov. 14, for an All Progressives Congress (APC) political rally at Zaria Road Stadium, where he acknowledged the suffering of communities affected by recurring attacks and displacement. Addressing residents and party supporters, Tinubu asked Plateau residents to forgive him for not visiting affected communities during his previous trip to the state in April. “When I last visited the other time, I was limited to the airport,” he said. “Forgive me if you didn’t see me in the hinterland, but I saw the devastation. I got the report from the governor. I saw horror in the faces of our people.” The president promised to rebuild communities destroyed by violence and facilitate the return of displaced residents. “We will rebuild your communities, and we will bring you back to your communities,” Tinbu added. “I have directed all the security agencies to take decisive action and sustain peace and stability on the Plateau.” He also commended the Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Dr. Bernard Doro, for identifying vulnerable populations and coordinating humanitarian assistance. Tinubu announced that 1,000 forest guards were undergoing training and that surveillance cameras promised to Plateau state had been procured to strengthen security monitoring and early warning operations. However, fresh attacks were reported within hours of the president’s departure from the state. In Mangu Local Government Area, armed attackers invaded Zwagal community in Jipal District at about 9 p.m. on Sunday, killing nine people. Other residents were reportedly missing following the attack. Silas Nanfwang, a resident who confirmed the incident to journalists, called on security agencies to intensify efforts to locate the attackers and bring those responsible to justice. In Barkin Ladi, 79-year-old Da Ishaku Pam Vwos was killed when armed men invaded Sho village at about 5:20 p.m. on Sunday, according to the Berom Youth Moulders Association (BYM). The association’s National Publicity Secretary, Rwang Tengwong, also reported the killing of 42-year-old Dauda John Davou during an attack on the Sambak community in Hoss District, Riyom LGA, at about 2 a.m. on Sunday. Another attack was reported in the Jol community around 12:10 a.m. on Sunday. According to BYM, local vigilantes responded to the attackers, preventing further casualties. The association said the incidents followed the shooting of Joshua Doro Dafwel in Jol on Wednesday. He is currently receiving medical attention. BYM also reported that Ina Arin was killed when armed men ambushed him and his friend, Abok Gyang, as they returned to Dorong village in Foron District. Gyang survived the attack. In Bokkos Local Government Area, two people, including a unit commander of the Plateau state-owned security outfit, Operation Rainbow, were killed in an ambush on Monday afternoon. The victims, identified as Gambo and his companion, were traveling on a motorcycle from Hurti village to Tadai in Manguna District when armed men attacked them at about 1:30 p.m. They had reportedly visited Hurti for a condolence visit and died at the scene. title: Hindu Nationalists Target Christians in West Bengal, India
summary: At least 48 to 65 incidents of targeted harassment, church vandalism, and physical violence against Christian communities in West Bengal, India, have been recorded between May and November. The Bangiy
content: At least 48 to 65 incidents of targeted harassment, church vandalism, and physical violence against Christian communities in West Bengal, India, have been recorded between May and November. The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba, a Christian organization working for the welfare of the state’s Christian community, compiled this data. The right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power in West Bengal following the April 2026 Legislative Assembly elections. Independent tracking by the research group India Hate Lab verified 60 hate crime incidents explicitly targeting Christian individuals, domestic fellowships, and institutional properties within West Bengal during the same period, confirming the widespread geographic footprint of the escalation of attacks on Christians. According to reports, the latest attack occurred on Nov. 9, when vandals desecrated a sacred shrine and Marian grotto of a church in an overnight attack in Khari Bamuner Chak, located within the Raidighi and Baruipur pastoral region of West Bengal’s South Parganas. A week earlier, a heavily organized contingent of about 40 men attacked a house prayer fellowship in Rayan village of the Bardhaman area. The assailants stormed the private residence during a morning service, violently assaulting the officiating pastor and worshippers. Surge of Attacks The surge in targeted violence, intimidation, and vandalism against Christian communities, churches, and home prayer fellowships in West Bengal is proving that Hindu nationalists have found West Bengal to be the new hunting ground with tacit support of the authorities. The state is currently experiencing a rapid breakdown in local law enforcement deterrence. This erosion directly threatens the constitutional guarantees enshrined in Article 25 of the Indian Constitution, which ensures freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion. The emergence of organized Hindutva networks operating with near-total impunity represents not merely localized social friction, but a systemic challenge to the rule of law and civil stability across the state. Faith Space Shrinking Across rural and semi-urban districts of West Bengal, Hindu nationalists increasingly employ physical blockades, structural desecration, and coordinated mob actions to shrink the space for religious minority assemblies. By weaponizing social intimidation and exploiting police inertia, these actors seek to criminalize ordinary acts of devotion, transforming private exercise of faith into contested public security triggers. Detailed documentation by human rights organizations and community defense networks attributes the vast majority of these incursions to organized Hindutva-affiliated groups. Investigations specifically point to operational coordination by local cadres associated with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) and the Bajrang Dal, the RSS’s militant arm. Assailants consistently deploy dual narratives of illegal “unlawful religious conversions” and fabricated “honey traps.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . The Kuala Lumpur High Court has ordered that a lawsuit filed by a…   The post  Malaysian Court Sends Christian Convert’s Religious Freedom Suit to Regional Bench  first appeared on  International Christian Conc
content: A 34-year-old law graduate’s multi-year battle exposes the severe reality of religious control and the legal trap facing citizens who want to leave Islam. A high-stakes constitutional challenge highlighting the erosion of religious freedom in Malaysia has taken a procedural step backward. The Kuala Lumpur High Court has ordered that a lawsuit filed by a 34-year-old legal researcher seeking legal recognition as a Christian be transferred to the Shah Alam High Court. The case lays bare the rigid and intrusive control exercised by state apparatuses and Islamic religious authorities over personal faith, showcasing a system where basic human rights — such as choosing one’s own religion — are tightly policed by the government. A Life Labeled Without Consent The plaintiff, Shameer PV, identifies as a Christian and has lived as one since he was 18. However, under strict Malaysian administrative regulations, the word “Islam” was stamped on his compulsory national identity card (MyKad) when he was just 12, following a bureaucratic policy introduced under the National Registration Act. Despite decades of personal conviction and his marriage to a Christian wife, the state continues to legally treat him as a Muslim, directly violating his parental and marital status and refusing to recognize his family. Shameer’s legal challenge names the federal government, the Selangor state government, and the Selangor Islamic Religious Council (MAIS) as defendants. He argues that labeling citizens by religion on state identity cards violates Article 11(1) of the Federal Constitution, which ostensibly guarantees every person the right to profess and practice their religion. Trapped in Shariah Bureaucracy Shameer’s ordeal underscores the labyrinthine and punishing hurdles forced upon religious minorities and converts in Malaysia’s dual-justice system, which runs a parallel set of Islamic (Shariah) courts alongside the civil judiciary. In 2018, Shameer initiated proceedings in a Selangor Shariah court seeking official recognition of his Christian faith. After an exhausting 72 court sessions spanning over seven years, the Shariah court dismissed his application in January. Rather than allowing him to move on with his life, the religious court went a step further, ordering state departments and Islamic authorities to “guide and control” his practice of Islam — effectively treating his desire to leave the faith as a disciplinary or correctional matter. Having exhausted the religious tribunal system, Shameer turned to the civil high court in July, filing an originating summons to ask the highest judicial authorities whether state-mandated religious labeling on identity cards is unconstitutional, and whether Shariah courts have any lawful jurisdiction over individuals who do not practice Islam. A Wider Crisis for Freedom of Conscience International human rights observers and religious freedom advocates have long criticized Malaysia’s legal framework regarding apostasy and conversion. While the Malaysian Constitution theoretically protects freedom of religion, civil courts have repeatedly ruled that only Islamic Shariah courts have the authority to permit someone to leave Islam — creating an effective judicial catch-22, as Shariah courts rarely grant permission to renounce the religion. For international human rights advocates and supporters of religious liberty, Shameer’s case is a stark reminder of the state-enforced religious controls facing millions in Southeast Asia. As his case moves to the Shah Alam court, the legal battle continues to test whether Malaysia’s secular constitutional framework can protect an individual’s fundamental right of conscience against a totalizing state religious bureaucracy. title: Teenage Girl Dies After Six Months in Captivity
summary: On Nov. 1, six people took their first steps of freedom after being held by Fulani extremists for more than six months. One of them died only two days later. Hasana Bulus, 13, died in the hospital where she was taken in critical condition. Bulus was one of the 11 people who were kidnapped by a Fulani militia in…   The post  Teenage Girl Dies After Six Months in Captivity  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On Nov. 1, six people took their first steps of freedom after being held by Fulani extremists for more than six months. One of them died only two days later. Hasana Bulus, 13, died in the hospital where she was taken in critical condition. Bulus was one of the 11 people who were kidnapped by a Fulani militia in April. One had escaped, but five died at the camp, and the rest were released with Bulus — including the 4-year-old daughter of a woman who had died in captivity. Bulus’ village, Awon, is predominantly Christian and has been the target of Fulani attacks, just like Ariko, a neighboring village in Kaduna state. According to a six-year study conducted by the Observatory for Religious Freedom in Africa (ORFA), Islamic Fulani militias are by far the deadliest persecutors of Christians in Nigeria. Ariko is home to the 37 Christians who were kidnapped during the Easter services earlier this year in a neighboring village. Of these, 17 people have died in captivity, 12 have escaped, and eight have since been released. The abductees from both these villages were held in the same forest hideout, where they were kept in inhumane conditions. “They [the villagers] told us how they would stay for two weeks without food,” one woman, whose father died in the camp, told Open Doors . “They only boil water to drink. That’s how they struggled before the bandits gave them corn flour, and they started making swallow (a porridge). The men are restrained, chained in groups; they are not free to move around.” All of the male abductees in these groups had died in the camp. Christian Solidarity Worldwide (CSW) is calling for Nigerian authorities to protect these communities and fight to free more people left in bondage. “We continue to urge the Nigerian government at state and federal levels to prioritize the protection of vulnerable communities throughout the nation, to combat the threat posed by the litany of terrorist groups that are active in the country far more effectively, and to secure the release of all abductees,” CSW CEO Scot Bower said. “Nigeria’s Christians do not need another statement of sympathy,” ICC’s president, Shawn Wright, said. “They need protection , justice , and accountability . When those who murder innocent Christians face no meaningful consequences, impunity becomes an invitation to the next attack. The Nigerian government must protect vulnerable communities, pursue the perpetrators, and make clear that these crimes will not go unanswered.” Story by Bella Agnello To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: Al-Shabab Kills 5 Christians in Mandera, Kenya
summary: On the morning of Nov. 10, gunfire shattered the quiet along the Mandera-Arabia road in the Hagarsu area of Mandera County, Kenya. Somali-based al-Shabab militants ambushed Christian construction workers inspecting a road project. The workers, who were non-locals, were targeted because of their identity and faith. A driver and the two police reservists assigned to…   The post  Al-Shabab Kills 5 Christians in Mandera, Kenya  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On the morning of Nov. 10, gunfire shattered the quiet along the Mandera-Arabia road in the Hagarsu area of Mandera County, Kenya. Somali-based al-Shabab militants ambushed Christian construction workers inspecting a road project. The workers, who were non-locals, were targeted because of their identity and faith. A driver and the two police reservists assigned to protect them were also killed. Eight people in total were killed, with the attack following a pattern of al-Shabab-linked violence in Kenya’s northeastern borderlands. “The attack was swift but intense, leaving many traumatized, but even though we walk through the valley of the shadow of death, we will fear no evil, for Jesus is with us; His rod and staff, they comfort us,” an eyewitness said. “That’s where we draw our confidence from regardless of the present circumstances.” A Persistent Danger Mandera County lies along Kenya’s border with Somalia. For Christians living in the region, insecurity is a reality. Christians who move into the area for work are vulnerable. Churches operate under constant threat; believers travel cautiously, pastors limit evening gatherings, and congregations often worship with one eye on the door. Even traveling to work can expose Christians to danger. “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; but Jesus said, ‘I have come that they may have life, and have it to the full,’” a local church leader said. “We are becoming more vigilant and yet committed to the preaching of the gospel in the face of this constant threat from the Islamic fighters.” Always a Target Al-Shabab has repeatedly targeted Christians in the northeastern region, particularly those perceived as outsiders and those who do not share the group’s extremist religious ideology. Converts from Islam to Christianity remain especially vulnerable to intimidation, threats, and violence. The police reservists assigned to protect the workers also lost their lives. “The word of God declared that we should not grow weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up,” an eyewitness who wished to remain anonymous said. “We therefore bury the dead and comfort the widows, but we refuse to stop gathering in his name and preaching the gospel of salvation.” Responding to the killing of the five Christians, another church leader requested prayers and support for the believers in Mandera and the families of the victims. “We call upon the global church to stand with persecuted believers in Kenya and pray for the families of those killed, the wounded, and Christians across Mandera,” he said. “Pray for the protection of Christian workers, pastors, and congregations, and that they will have the courage to continue worshipping and sharing the gospel. Pray for lasting peace. The church in Mandera is not forgotten. Let us stand with them.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . title: At Least 26 Killed in DRC’s Mambasa Territory Amid Ebola Crisis
summary: Twenty-six people have reportedly been killed and several others abducted in a new attack carried out by the Islamist rebels of Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) on Nov. 10, during the night, in Mambasa territory, Ituri province, northeastern DR Congo, a country where nearly 93% of the population is Christian. According to a local association coordinator, Malikidogo, more…   The post  At Least 26 Killed in DRC’s Mambasa Territory Amid Ebola Crisis  first appeared on  International Christian Concern
content: Twenty-six people have reportedly been killed and several others abducted in a new attack carried out by the Islamist rebels of Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) on Nov. 10, during the night, in Mambasa territory, Ituri province, northeastern DR Congo, a country where nearly 93% of the population is Christian. According to a local association coordinator, Malikidogo, more than six villages were affected, including Kangwayi, Misele, Mingazi, and Mambaka. “The situation is very serious; we identified 26 people killed, several others abducted, and many families are still searching for their missing loved ones,” Malikidogo said. “Aside from the death of many people, five houses were burnt alongside some motorcycles. We are calling on the authorities to take urgent action to protect the population.” Left With Nothing Survivors who succeeded in escaping reported that many families had to run for their lives, leaving their homes and belongings behind. “We were very afraid when we realized that the enemies were already in the village when we heard people crying and others running in every direction,” one survivor said. “We just fled without having time to collect our belongings, just to save our lives. We do not know what will happen next, and we are afraid that they might come and reach Mambasa city where we are today.” The attack comes at a difficult time for local communities, which are already facing the threat of Ebola . Residents are now dealing with both the fear of the disease and the danger of further attacks. There are concerns that the violence could also make it harder to control the Ebola outbreak. People fleeing their villages may spread the disease to other communities, while insecurity could prevent health workers from reaching those who need medical help. A local leader also expressed concern about the situation and called for stronger protection of civilians. “We have suffered for many years because of the atrocities committed by ADF Islamist terrorists,” he said. “We are already struggling with Ebola, and now we are facing these attacks again. We cannot continue living like this. We are calling on the government and security forces to protect our communities before more innocent lives are lost.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: 4 Killed Days After Cantine Massacre
summary: Just days after the deadly massacre in Cantine, where at least 33 civilians were reportedly killed, suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have struck again in Beni Territory, claiming four more lives and burning several houses in Mabalako, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. At about 12:20 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, Mabalako once again…   The post  4 Killed Days After Cantine Massacre  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Just days after the deadly massacre in Cantine, where at least 33 civilians were reportedly killed, suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have struck again in Beni Territory, claiming four more lives and burning several houses in Mabalako, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. At about 12:20 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, Mabalako once again faced ADF violence , with a fresh overnight attack in the Kamahume neighborhood. According to local civil society representatives, the death toll rose from an initial three to four, while more than seven houses were also set ablaze during the deadly incursion. The attack has renewed fears among civilians already traumatized by the violence that struck Cantine-Aloya less than a week earlier. The proximity of these two attacks in time and location has heightened concerns about the continuing threat posed by the ADF to civilian populations across Beni. “We are living in constant fear,” said Mulwahali, a survivor. “We have not yet recovered from the pain of what happened in Cantine, where innocent people were brutally killed and homes reduced to ashes. Now the violence has reached Mabalako, and once again we are mourning our loved ones and watching our homes burn. We do not know who will be next or where these attackers will strike again. We are even tired of burying our people without heads. All we want is to live in peace and sleep in our homes without fearing that we may never see another morning.” A Need for Security Local civil society representatives have appealed to security services to take full responsibility for protecting civilians, strengthen security operations, and prevent further attacks. Residents of Runzayi, Malondo, Ngazi, and Kibunamaru have also been urged to remain vigilant, maintain calm, and cooperate with security forces by reporting suspicious movements. “We cannot continue living at the mercy of armed attackers,” a local Catholic bishop said. “Although the intervention of the FARDC helped limit the destruction in Mabalako, the fact that the attackers could strike and disappear without their direction being known leaves us deeply frightened. We want security, not another massacre.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . title: The Girl They Killed for Refusing a Forced Marriage
summary: On Nov. 6, an 18-year-old Christian girl named Ajak Mabior was beaten to death in Jonglei, South Sudan, after refusing to enter a forced marriage arranged by her family. She was expected to marry an older Muslim man — a marriage she opposed because of her Christian faith and her unwillingness to be forced into it. After…   The post  The Girl They Killed for Refusing a Forced Marriage  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On Nov. 6, an 18-year-old Christian girl named Ajak Mabior was beaten to death in Jonglei, South Sudan, after refusing to enter a forced marriage arranged by her family. She was expected to marry an older Muslim man — a marriage she opposed because of her Christian faith and her unwillingness to be forced into it. After attempting to escape, she was killed by her own brother and cousin. Days later, police in Bor arrested the two men but released them without charges after family members demanded their freedom, arguing that “there was no case” because they were relatives. A Common Problem The killing has raised serious concerns among Christian leaders about the pressure Christian girls face when their faith and personal convictions conflict with family expectations. “When a young girl is killed for refusing a forced marriage, and the killers walk free because they are family, the message is clear: Tradition is stronger than the law, and stronger than the value of a life,” a local pastor said. “Many of our Christian daughters live under this same shadow.” For Christian girls in South Sudan , forced marriages can become a matter of religious persecution when they are pressured to marry outside their faith and abandon their Christian convictions. Those who refuse may face rejection, threats, intimidation, and violence from their own families. Mabior’s death highlights the vulnerability of young Christian women who seek to remain faithful to Christ while facing pressure to submit to marriages that violate their faith and conscience. “The church teaches that every life is precious because it is created in the image of God,” the pastor added. “Yet when a Christian girl refuses a marriage that would bind her against her will, she can be treated as a traitor to the community. We have buried too many who paid that price.” Seeking Justice The authorities’ response has added to the church’s concerns. Police reportedly released the suspects without the consent of the Jonglei State Caretaker Commissioner. The justification that the suspects were relatives raises serious questions about the protection available to Christian girls facing forced marriages and violence. When perpetrators are released without facing justice, vulnerable Christian women are left with little confidence that the authorities will protect their right to practice their faith and make decisions according to their conscience. “We preach freedom in Christ, but our young people still live in fear of the consequences of that freedom,” the pastor said. “If the police and local authorities remain quiet, the church becomes the only place left where these girls and boys can find a voice. We need courage to speak, and we need the wider Body of Christ to stand with us.” Mabior’s case raises concerns about forced interfaith marriages, religious pressure, and violence against young Christian women in South Sudan. “We call on the wider Body of Christ to pray for Ajak’s justice, and for the protection of Christian girls facing forced marriages because of their faith,” an International Christian Concern (ICC) staffer said. “Pray that the church will have the courage to speak against religious coercion and violence, and that the authorities will uphold the law and protect vulnerable believers.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: Ansaru Militants Claim Killing of Muslim Cleric Who Preached Peace with Christians
summary: Ansaru militants have claimed responsibility for shooting dead a Muslim cleric known for promoting peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims, raising fresh concerns about the threats facing religious voices who challenge extremist ideologies in Nigeria. Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka and his friend, Adamu Abubakar, were killed Monday evening, Oct. 26, in Dutsin-Ma Local Government…   The post  Ansaru Militants Claim Killing of Muslim Cleric Who Preached Peace with Christians  first ap
content: Ansaru militants have claimed responsibility for shooting dead a Muslim cleric known for promoting peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims, raising fresh concerns about the threats facing religious voices who challenge extremist ideologies in Nigeria. Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka and his friend, Adamu Abubakar, were killed Monday evening, Oct. 26, in Dutsin-Ma Local Government Area of Katsina state. Two armed men riding a motorcycle reportedly opened fire on the men outside the cleric’s residence before fleeing. The Nigeria Police in Katsina confirmed the killing. The Nigerian government condemned the killings on Tuesday, while Ansaru subsequently claimed responsibility in an audio message, accusing Masussuka of being an infidel and opposing Islam. Masussuka had used social media to share Islamic teachings in Hausa, a major language spoken across northern Nigeria. In some of his videos, he called on Muslims to stop describing Christians as infidels and urged followers of both religions to live together peacefully. His message challenged religious hostility at a time when Christian communities in parts of Nigeria continue to face deadly attacks from armed extremist groups. For Christians who heard his teachings, Masussuka’s appeal for coexistence offered a reminder that resistance to religious hatred can also come from within the Muslim community. His killing has raised questions about whether those who challenge extremist interpretations of religion can safely express their views. Ansaru Accuses Cleric of Opposing Islam In an audio message released Tuesday, Oct. 27, Ansaru claimed it attacked at about 8:30 p.m. The speaker reportedly referred to Tuesday as the day of the killing, although the deaths were reported to have occurred on Monday evening. The group’s description of Masussuka as an infidel is significant because the cleric had reportedly used his platform to challenge the practice of labeling Christians in that way; the accusation against him raises concerns about the risks faced by people whose religious teachings conflict with extremist beliefs. Masussuka’s friend, Abubakar, was killed in the same shooting. Publicly available information about Abubakar’s life, his relationship with the cleric, and whether the attackers specifically targeted either man remains limited. Their deaths have left two families grieving and a community seeking answers about why the men were killed. Ansaru, formerly known as Jama’atu Ansarul Muslimina Fi Biladis Sudan, is a Nigerian jihadist organization that emerged as a breakaway faction of Boko Haram around 2012. The group has longstanding links to al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb, an al-Qaida affiliate active in the Sahel and North Africa. Ansaru has been associated with kidnappings, hostage killings, and attacks against security personnel and other targets. The United States designated the group a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2013. Ansaru is one of several armed extremist organizations operating within Nigeria’s wider security crisis. Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) have carried out attacks on Christian worshippers, churches and predominantly Christian communities, as well as killings of Muslim civilians and others they consider opponents. These groups are distinct, and responsibility for each attack must be established through evidence. Nevertheless, their activities have contributed to a climate in which religious communities fear violence, displacement and the loss of loved ones. For Nigerian Christians, the danger extends beyond individual killings. Attacks on communities, places of worship and religious leaders can disrupt church activities, force families from their homes and leave survivors struggling to rebuild their lives.
