title: No Condemnation
summary: Featuring thousands of study notes drawn from the bestselling NIV Application Commentary series, the NIV Application Bible helps you understand Scripture and connect it to your world in a whole new way. It guides you in discovering how the ancient truths found in Scripture relate to your experiences today using insight from trusted evangelical scholars, paired with timely biblical application principles. Read an excerpt on the blog. See Also Free Stuff Fridays (HarperCollins) Using the NIV Zonde
content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Zondervan and this article is adapted from the NIV Application Bible . Text in bold is taken from the application notes on Romans 8:1 in the NIV Application Bible. Beneath the outer veneer of our lives, many of us live with a layer of guilt and shame. We feel like we’re not good enough. We want to be good Christians, but we just don’t feel like we are. Perhaps we sit in church surrounded by people who seem to have their lives more together than ours and who seem to lead better Christian lives than we do. This feeling leaves us anxious and ashamed, unsure of where we really stand before God. Let Romans 8:1 fill you with hope: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”! Because we are justified by faith in Christ, we escape the sentence of spiritual death that our sins have earned. We have been transferred into the new realm of life. Because we have believed in Jesus’ finished work for us on the cross, we no longer have to fear that our sins will ever condemn us. Once we are walking with Jesus, we walk by faith and depend on grace rather than our own works. Our hope is not in what we have done or in what we can do, but in what God has done in Christ Jesus through his death and resurrection. If we are in Christ, there is no condemnation. If God does not condemn us, we must not go on condemning ourselves. Instead, we walk in the freedom and joy of God’s grace, led by God’s Holy Spirit. title: Who or What? A Continuum for Using AI Wisely
summary: From AI as god to AI as assistant. Here is a continuum of nine roles that can help Christians tell legitimate uses of AI from illegitimate ones, and wise from unwise. See Also A Christian’s Guide to AI Technology is Fast, Sanctification Is Slow, and Claude Can’t Do It For You A La Carte (October 16)
content: It is sometimes hard to believe that it has been only four years since AI became widely available. Few technologies have made so massive and rapid a leap into our daily lives, to the extent that AI now exists in the background of all of our lives and, for many of us, in the foreground as well. Few technologies have evolved as quickly, so that the latest ChatGPT model bears about as much resemblance to its debut as the latest MacBook does to a Commodore 64. If all this has happened in just four years, imagine what the next four—or the next fourteen—might hold. As AI’s capabilities have increased, so too have the ways we can use it in our homes, churches, and workplaces. It seems like every month or two we read of a feature that can make a difference to our lives by adding a new ability or taking on work that used to be done by a person. The latest trend is the rise of agents—AI tools like Meta’s Muse or xAI’s Grok Bot that can carry out tasks, routines, and duties on an ongoing basis. With all of the tools available to us and all of their capabilities, it can be difficult to know which uses are legitimate and which are not. We all know that just because AI can do a task doesn’t mean that it should . So how can we determine the legitimate roles AI can play in our lives? I think sketching out a continuum of some of AI’s potential roles can help us. At the beginning are roles that most of us would agree are illegitimate, and at the end roles that most of us would agree are legitimate. Between them are roles that may be illegitimate in some cases and perfectly fine in others. These demand that we approach them thoughtfully to determine whether integrating them into our lives would be an act of wisdom or folly. As you will see, illegitimate roles tend to be those that require a who whereas legitimate roles tend to be those that require a mere what . The Continuum AI as God . There are some people, most of them deeply engaged in the tech industry, who ascribe to AI god-like qualities and who relate to it accordingly. They may believe it is an evil god that is likely to destroy humanity or a benevolent god that is likely to redeem humanity, but in either case, they treat AI as something far more than software. These people go too far and commit idolatry as they attribute to tech what rightly belongs to God. AI as Friend . There are some people who relate to AI as a friend, and even a few troubled people who relate to it as a lover. While AI is capable of mimicking the kind of relationship one might enjoy with a fellow human being, it can only ever mimic it. To relate to AI as a friend is to anthropomorphize a mere technology and worse, to deprive oneself of actual friendship. Though AI can imitate friendship, it cannot be a friend in any legitimate sense of the word, for friendship depends upon personhood. Not only that, but friendship depends upon mutuality and both the blessings and risks that come with relationship. You cannot be friends with AI any more than you can be friends with a tree, a PlayStation, or any other non-being. AI as Counselor . Many people today relate to AI as a counselor—a confidant who will listen patiently and counsel them with a trusted voice. Yet because AI is a what , not a who , it cannot offer answers based on a true understanding of their circumstances, true wisdom that comes from learning and experience, or true compassion that comes from sharing their humanity. It cannot empathize with them, pray for them, or plead with the Holy Spirit for wisdom in helping them. AI is capable of advising in many ways, but not of counseling, for counseling is inherently personal. AI as Pastor . Increasingly, people bring to AI the matters of spiritual health, growth, and well-being that in the past would have been addressed to a pastor. Every Christian needs to be under the loving oversight of a pastor who will care for their soul, and such crucial matters must be entrusted not to AI, but to a pastor who is called and

title: A La Carte (November 16)
summary: Can you keep falling into the same sin and still be a Christian? / Seven thoughts on how we change / To the man seconds away from watching porn / Does the Incarnation authorize images of Christ? / What is supernatural is not necessarily mystical / The heritage trees of the church / Kindle deals and more See Also A La Carte (December 23) A La Carte (November 13) A La Carte (October 24)
content: Good morning. Grace and peace to you. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include some seasonally appropriate choices from Crossway, like Come, Let Us Adore Him: A Daily Advent Devotional , Good News of Great Joy: 25 Devotional Readings for Advent , and Everyday Gospel Christmas Devotional . Remember that there’s a substantial November Kindle sale going on as well. If you prefer print books, then be sure to look at the Pre-Black Friday sale on a wide variety of books, many of them from Zondervan and Zondervan Academic. Recommended Reading Can You Keep Falling into the Same Sin and Still Be a Christian? This is a very good question and one all Christians need to ask when we assess our lives. “You’ve done it again. The very sin you promised yourself you wouldn’t commit. Perhaps it was an angry outburst. Another dishonest conversation. Another evening viewing pornography. Another moment of bitterness, gossip or pride. You knew it was wrong. You’d prayed about it. Perhaps you’d even confessed it to another Christian. Yet here you are again. And now a troubling question begins to form. ‘Can I really be a Christian if I keep falling into the same sin?'” Seven Thoughts on How We Change. This article by Jason Hsieh nicely complements the previous one. “Have you ever felt stuck on how to make progress with a particular struggle? Trying to change, repent, or grow in Christ can be a long, arduous road met with frustration, doubt, and discouragement. This post highlights seven factors that help us change. While it’s not exhaustive, it may give you and those whom you walk alongside ideas about what could be missing in your efforts.” To The Man Seconds Away From Watching Porn. And here’s one more piece on sin, though this one covers a specific form of sin. “The first germ of temptation drifted down long ago. Gradually, like snow gathering on a tree branch, the weight has quietly grown heavy, so very heavy; you feel you cannot hold it back any longer. So, here you are: browsing the Internet, hoping to ‘stumble’ upon something, anything, that will give you a justifiable excuse for succumbing. The dark monster of Lust is looking for an opportunity to swing you, branch to branch, from your typical Internet content to something more sinister, more secretive, more sensual.” Does the Incarnation Authorize Images of Christ? The issue of whether or not Christians should create images of Christ comes up often. Anthony Faggiano offers a very typically Reformed/Presbyterian response. “A recent discussion on X about a theological book cover raised a question that seems to come around every Holiday season. Reformed Christians objected to its picture of Christ. Roman Catholic participants raised an objection worth considering: because God became man, depicting Christ does not violate the Second Commandment. If God made himself visible at the Incarnation, why should Christians refuse to portray him? That honest question deserves a careful answer. Jesus truly became one of us. Yet I believe that his becoming visible didn’t give us permission to make pictures of him.” What is Supernatural is Not Necessarily Mystical. Michael Kelley distinguishes between the supernatural and the mystical. “Just because something is supernatural doesn’t necessarily mean it’s mystical. When we think of something being mystical, it’s a bit more hazy than something being supernatural. When we say something is mystical, we mean it’s obscure. It’s mysterious. And while the two words might share some characteristics, I’m thinking more and more that it’s important for us to recognize the difference because doing so impacts the way we live out our faith.” The Heritage Trees of the Church. title: Works & Wonders (November 15)
summary: This week’s Works & Wonders: a devotional on God’s sovereignty, Voyager’s light-day, Indelible Grace’s Draw Near, the Pano Awards, Codex, and octopus escapes. See Also Works & Wonders (Oct 11) Works & Wonders (September 27) Works & Wonders (April 19)
content: In my weekly Works & Wonders column, I combine a brief devotional with other interesting and uplifting bits and pieces I gleaned throughout the week. I hope you enjoy this week’s collection! It includes: All Will Bow: A Devotional Voyager’s Light Day Draw Near Pano Awards Codex How Octopuses Squeeze Through Heal and Make Whole 1. All Will Bow God is often described as sovereign. “Sovereign” is a word of royalty or kingship that describes one who has supreme power and authority within his rightful jurisdiction—both the right and the ability to act in the ways he sees fit. A king has the right to act only within his own kingdom, yet because God created the world and owns it and fills it, his dominion extends through all time and all space—through all that is and all that will be. It extends even to each human being, for all have been created by God and all, therefore, owe allegiance to him. As sovereign, God has purposed to have all bow the knee to him, their rightful ruler. And through his power all will, though in different ways. Some will see his word and his works, respond to his mercy, and bow in worship. Some will see his word and works, harden their hearts, and be forced to bow before him in judgment. But either way, all will bow before him. 2. Voyager’s Light Day NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is about to mark its first “ light day ” as it reaches one light-day from earth—much farther than any human-made object has ever traveled. It will be 16 billion miles from Earth, having been launched in 1977. NASA has an invitation for you: after sunset on Tuesday, November 17, step outside and flash V-G-R in Morse code at the sky with a flashlight or phone, since VGR was Voyager’s call sign. While one light-day is a notable accomplishment, it may be worth pointing out that the edge of the observable universe is something like 47 billion light-years away, so we haven’t exactly caught up to the Lord. 3. Draw Near I didn’t see this one coming: the second Indelible Grace album of 2026. Yet here we have it: Draw Near . Like its predecessors, it is composed largely of retuned hymns from the past, though I believe there are some originals as well. (2026’s other album was Rove No More , in case you’d like to give it a listen as well.) 4. Pano Awards The photography competition of the week is the Pano Awards , which honors the best examples of panoramic photography. Panoramas will nearly always be landscapes, which is my favorite kind of photography. Not surprisingly, the results are stunning. 5. Codex Codex is a neat new initiative from the missions organization Missionary. I’ll allow the people who made it to explain it: “Codex is an index of unreached language groups (ULGs), people united by language yet strangers to Christ and His Church. By detailing who the unreached are, where they live, what they believe, and what stands between them and salvation, Codex fuels informed prayer for those who have not heard.” 6. How Octopuses Squeeze Through You’ve probably seen videos of octopuses squeezing through holes that seem far too small and, in fact, may be even narrower than the most rigid part of their body. Scientists recently put the effort into figuring out how they do it, and the answer is pretty interesting. Helpfully, they captured it all on video so you can see it for yourself. You’ll need to read Science News’s How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step to learn how they do it. 7. Heal and Make Whole I enjoyed this new live recording from of “ Heal and Make Whole ” from The Soil and Seed Project. It’s a whimsical telling of the life of Christ through trees. I guess you’ll need to give it a listen to figure out what that means. You can find the lyrics here if you scroll down. title: Cathedrals and Landmarks Lit in Red Worldwide as Red Week Draws Attention to Persecuted Christians
summary: PARIS—Churches and landmarks around the world are being lit in red this week for Red Week, an annual campaign to draw attention to the persecution of Christians, which its organizers say is worsening.
content: PARIS—Churches and landmarks around the world are being lit in red this week for Red Week, an annual campaign to draw attention to the persecution of Christians, which its organizers say is worsening. The campaign, which runs Nov. 15–22, is organized by the Catholic charity Aid to the Church in Need (ACN). It follows the charity’s Oct. 27 report, which found that conditions for Christians had worsened in 10 of the 18 countries examined and improved in none. Worldwide, more than 1,000 churches, including about 130 cathedrals, and other iconic buildings are taking part, according to the charity, which says the color recalls the blood of martyrs. They include U.S. churches such as Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Church in De Pere, Wisconsin, as well as Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, the Italian government’s seat at Palazzo Chigi in Rome, St. Peter’s Cathedral in Germany, Almudena Cathedral in Madrid, St. George’s Cathedral in London, and St. Mary’s Cathedral in Sydney. The European Parliament buildings in Strasbourg, in eastern France, are scheduled to be lit on Nov. 23. The campaign began in Brazil in 2015, when ACN’s local office had Rio de Janeiro’s Christ the Redeemer statue lit in red to draw attention to the persecution of Christians in Iraq. “Lighting these monuments in red is a fantastic way to draw attention to what Christians endure around the world,” Sylvie, 52, who teaches French at a high school in Rouen, in Normandy, told The Epoch Times as she watched Notre-Dame being lit in red. “Our media like to talk about the supposed plight of ‘minorities’ in the West, yet they barely mention the very real plight of Christians under Islamic or communist regimes,” she said. “And I say this as someone who is not a Christian.” Christian Persecution Worsens: Report The report “Persecuted and Forgotten?” covers the period from August 2024 to June 2026. The charity estimates that about 220 million Christians worldwide are directly exposed to persecution. The report cites Pew Research Center data showing that Christians were harassed in 165 countries in 2023, the highest figure for any religious group. “Objectively, the situation of Christians around the world is deteriorating, because the enemies of the Church are many,” Benoît de Blanpré, director of ACN’s French branch, told The Epoch Times. Among the threats he cited were Islamism, authoritarian communist regimes, and laws against conversion and proselytism. Iran and Islamist Violence in Africa In Iran, where conversion from Islam is illegal, 254 arrests of Christians were reported in 2025, about double the 2024 figure, according to the report. “The regime seeks to push Christians out of society, either by making them flee or by preventing them from living freely,” Blanpré said. He said an Iranian Christian who had become a French citizen was invited to share his story at an ACN vigil last year. However, he asked for his testimony to be read anonymously because he feared for his safety and that of his parents, who still live in Iran. According to the 2026 Global Terrorism Index, six of the 10 countries most affected by terrorism are in Africa. The ACN report says Islamist terrorists affiliated with the Islamic State and Al Qaeda control at least 40 percent of Burkina Faso. It also reports that Fulani herder militias killed more than 200 Christians in a single night in June 2025 in the Nigerian town of Yelewata. In some other Muslim-majority countries such as Algeria, Blanpré described the situation as “very difficult,” saying Christians there “are asked to make no noise, to take up no space, and to be as discreet as possible.” In Muslim-majority countries such as Qatar, apostasy, the act of renouncing Islam, is punishable by death under Sharia law. In others, such as Algeria, leaving Islam is not a criminal offense, but proselytizing to Muslims by non-Muslims is prohibited and can carry prison sentences of up to five years. Dal «fallimento salutare» che lo storico individua nel 7 ottobre alle fratture che attraversano oggi la società israeliana, l’intervista ripercorre la promessa del sionismo, la sovranità e la vulnerabilità ebraiche, l’accusa di colonialismo, il riemergere dell’odio antiebraico e il suo rapporto personale con la Francia. Al termine di questo lungo colloquio, Bensoussan formula una distinzione significativa: esprime fiducia nel futuro del sionismo, che concepisce come un processo di emancipazione dell’essere ebreo non conclusosi con la nascita dello Stato, ma considera più preoccupante la questione della stessa sopravvivenza dello Stato d’Israele, minacciata, a suo giudizio, innanzitutto dalle proprie fratture interne. Un’intervista approfondita, senza eludere le questioni più difficili, riletta integralmente dall’avvocato Michel Laval. Lei conclude ‘Una nuova storia del sionismo’ nel 1950. Se dovesse scrivere oggi il capitolo che inizia il 7 ottobre 2023, quale titolo gli darebbe? Senza alcuno spirito di sterile provocazione, lo intitolerei «un fallimento salutare», perché, come dopo il trauma della guerra del Kippur, esattamente cinquant’anni prima, il massacro genocidario del 7 ottobre 2023 ha indotto la società israeliana a interrogarsi su una certa arroganza, a rimettersi in discussione, dopo aver sottovalutato il nemico e sopravvalutato se stessa. È dallo shock seguito al Kippur del 1973, e naturalmente dalle trasformazioni della società israeliana, che è nata la svolta del 1977, quando per la prima volta l’opposizione di destra è arrivata al potere. Il suo libro racconta come un popolo vissuto in una condizione di dipendenza politica abbia deciso di tornare a essere soggetto della propria storia. Il 7 ottobre ha rivelato che la sovranità ebraica non aveva eliminato la vulnerabilità degli ebrei? La sovranità ebraica rappresentata dal sionismo politico non ha mai preteso di abolire la vulnerabilità degli ebrei. La sovranità dà vita a una nazione israeliana che non ha nulla a che vedere con il concetto di comunità ebraica. In altre parole, lo Stato d’Israele è uno Stato-nazione, non una comunità ebraica in più. L’assalto alla nave Altalena, nel giugno 1948, sulle spiagge di Tel Aviv, ne è un esempio. Ben Gurion ordina di sparare con i cannoni contro il mercantile noleggiato dall’Irgun di Menachem Begin, che intendeva riservare alla propria milizia una parte delle armi trasportate. title: El papa León XIV ya está en Argentina y el campo tuvo protagonismo en su primer discurso
summary: Tras pasar por Uruguay, el papa León XIV inició este domingo su histórica gira de cuatro días por Argentina, que constituye la primera llegada de un líder de la Iglesia Católica mundial a nuestro país
content: Tras pasar por Uruguay, el papa León XIV inició este domingo su histórica gira de cuatro días por Argentina, que constituye la primera llegada de un líder de la Iglesia Católica mundial a nuestro país desde Juan Pablo II en 1987. En ese marco, la primera actividad del Sumo Pontífice fue un discurso en el Palacio Libertad de la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires (CABA), frente al presidente de la Nación, Javier Milei. Y aunque sus palabras lógicamente estuvieron apuntadas hacia toda la sociedad, hubo numerosos pasajes que encontraron especial sintonía con el mundo agropecuario. Esto, en la previa de la reunión que León XIV mantendrá el lunes con representantes empresariales, sindicales y de organizaciones sociales, entre los que estarán los presidentes de las cuatro entidades de la Mesa de Enlace. EL PAPA LEÓN XIV EN ARGENTINA Puntualmente, el jefe mayor del Vaticano destacó el valor del esfuerzo cotidiano de los argentinos, con una mención expresa a quienes trabajan en el campo, y reivindicó la importancia de generar oportunidades, estimular la iniciativa privada y aprovechar responsablemente los recursos naturales. “Esta tierra conoce bien el valor del esfuerzo de quienes se ganan la vida en el campo y en las ciudades”, expresó León XIV, al destacar también el papel de los emprendedores y de las familias que sostienen sus hogares a través del trabajo. Asimismo, el Papa reconoció el enorme potencial productivo del país, al señalar que la Argentina cuenta con una extraordinaria riqueza natural, desde sus campos y reservas de agua hasta sus fuentes de energía, minerales y biodiversidad. Así, su mensaje combinó la posibilidad de aprovechar esos recursos para generar desarrollo y bienestar con la responsabilidad de preservar el ambiente y las condiciones de vida de las futuras generaciones. También dedicó un espacio a la innovación, la investigación y las nuevas tecnologías, incluida la inteligencia artificial, destacando su capacidad para transformar la producción y mejorar la vida de las personas. Por otro lado, al expresar una mirada sobre América del Sur, mencionó además a los alimentos, la energía y el conocimiento como elementos que vinculan a los países y abren oportunidades para fortalecer la cooperación regional. LEON XIV, EL MARTÍN FIERO Y EL MATE Asimismo, León XIV ofreció referencias cargadas de simbolismo para la identidad argentina. Por ejemplo, mencionó al Martín Fierro de José Hernández, a Jorge Luis Borges, al tango y a las tradiciones del interior del país. Y no faltó una de las costumbres más arraigadas entre los argentinos: el mate compartido, al que presentó como un gesto cotidiano que favorece la conversación y la cercanía. Por último, hacia el final de su intervención, León XIV evocó a Nuestra Señora de Luján, patrona de la Argentina y figura de especial significado para las comunidades rurales y para generaciones de familias de todo el país. También recordó al papa Francisco, citó a Carlos Gardel y alentó a los argentinos a valorar el patrimonio recibido de las generaciones anteriores y trabajar para dejar un país mejor a quienes vendrán. De esta manera, sin ser un discurso específicamente dirigido al agro, las palabras de León XIV dejaron un reconocimiento al trabajo rural, a la producción, a la iniciativa emprendedora y a las tradiciones que forman parte de la identidad argentina. Un mensaje que también llegó al corazón del campo argentino. EL DISCURSO COMPLETO DEL PAPA LEÓN XIV Señor Presidente de la República, distinguidas autoridades y miembros del cuerpo diplomático. Señoras y señores, me alegra profundamente encontrarme hoy en esta querida tierra argentina. Saludos también a los miembros del cuerpo diplomático y a las demás autoridades aquí presentes, y extiendo con afecto mi saludo a todos los argentinos. title: Papa Leone : Lautorità intesa come servizio è orientata al bene comune
summary: Primo discorso della seconda tappa del viaggio apostolico di Papa Leone XIV in Sud America. Parlando al Palacio Libertad a Buenos Aires, di fronte alle autorità, alla società civile e al corpo diploma
content: Primo discorso della seconda tappa del viaggio apostolico di Papa Leone XIV in Sud America. Parlando al Palacio Libertad a Buenos Aires, di fronte alle autorità, alla società civile e al corpo diplomatico argentini, il Santo Padre ha ricordato che ogni generazione riceve ine eredità dalla precedente il proprio Paese e a sua volta partecipa alla sua costruzione, imparando a discernere cosa va conservato. Il patrimonio comune, ha aggiunto Leone, comprende anche la democrazia, che chiede all’autorità di intendere il proprio compito come servizio orientato al bene comune a partire dalle condizioni concrete della vita delle persone, come le famiglie e i giovani, che devono poter ricevere opportunità professionali ed educazione per realizzare i propri progetti di vita senza il peso dell’incertezza o dover andare altrove. Il saluto “Signor Presidente della Repubblica, distinte Autorità e membri del Corpo diplomatico, Signore e Signori,sono molto lieto di trovarmi oggi in questa cara Terra argentina. La ringrazio, Signor Presidente, per le cordiali parole che ha voluto rivolgermi e per l’accoglienza che, attraverso di Lei, mi riserva il suo Popolo. Saluto inoltre i membri del Corpo diplomatico e le altre Autorità presenti, ed estendo con affetto il mio saluto a tutti gli Argentini. “Sono venuto come Successore dell’Apostolo Pietro e, pertanto, come Pastore. Desidero incontrare la Chiesa in cammino in questa Terra e rivolgermi anche all’intera Nazione e a coloro ai quali è stato affidato il compito di servirla. La Chiesa accompagna la vita dei popoli attraverso la missione che le è stata affidata. Per questo, anche nei confronti di coloro che ricoprono cariche pubbliche, desidera offrire una parola ispirata al Vangelo e volta a tutelare la dignità di ogni persona, la concordia e il bene comune“. Un’ampia storia “Venire in questa terra ha, per me, un significato particolare. Per dodici anni la Chiesa universale ha ascoltato la voce di un Pontefice argentino, che ha portato con sé, nella memoria e nel cuore, i luoghi, le persone e la fede che qui ha ricevuto. Oggi, succedendogli nel Ministero petrino, percorro in un certo senso la strada inversa e vengo nella Patria dove Papa Francesco ha iniziato un cammino, che in seguito si sarebbe intrecciato con quello di tutta la Chiesa. Avvicinarmi alla terra in cui è cresciuto significa anche avvicinarmi a una storia molto più ampia, fatta di generazioni di uomini e donne che, prima e dopo di lui, hanno accolto questa Patria e vi hanno lasciato qualcosa di sé. Alcuni sono nati qui; altri sono giunti da lontano e vi hanno trovato una casa; altri ancora appartengono a popoli indigeni, la cui presenza precede la nascita della Nazione. Da quell’incontro fra origini ed esperienze diverse ha preso forma, col passare del tempo, un Popolo che ha saputo aprire le proprie porte, fare spazio a chi arrivava e mantenere, anche nei momenti difficili, una notevole capacità di rialzarsi e andare avanti. Tutti hanno contribuito a plasmare l’Argentina che oggi ho la gioia di visitare”. Il patrimonio comune “Nessuna generazione costruisce la Patria partendo da zero. La riceve. Lo fa attraverso una lingua e legami che l’hanno preceduta; attraverso istituzioni fondate da altri e beni che sono cresciuti grazie al lavoro di molti. La storia custodisce motivi di gratitudine, ma anche ricordi dolorosi. content: Antes de escribir la biografía de Jorge Bergoglio, que llamó El gran Reformador, Austen Ivereigh ya era un experto en la historia de la Iglesia argentina. “Mi tesis de doctorado [en Oxford], que terminé en el 92, fue sobre catolicismo y política en la Argentina”. Y hay más: “Debo mi fe a la Iglesia Argentina, leyendo artículos de monseñor (Gustavo) Franceschi, volví a la fe”, dice. Ese conocimiento de nuestro país y de su fe mayoritaria representó una ventaja a la hora de escribir sobre Bergoglio, ya que cada etapa de la trayectoria del futuro Papa está debidamente contextualizada en la época que atravesaba el país. Desde aquel marzo de 2013, cuando la novedad de un pontífice argentino y jesuita impactó al mundo entero, Ivereihg siempre pensó que vendría cuando Francisco visitara la Argentina, viaje que finalmente no se concretó. “Ahora vengo con León”, comenta. En efecto, este escritor, historiador, periodista y analista de asuntos religiosos y políticos estará en nuestro país contemporáneamente con la visita del papa León XIV, invitado por la Universidad del Salvador (USAL), donde dictó, el pasado viernes 6, una clase magistral sobre “El giro latinoamericano Francisco-León: la Iglesia misionera sinodal y el cambio de época”. Ivereigh también es co-autor de Let Us Dream (Soñemos Juntos, 2020), un libro escrito en colaboración con Francisco. Su trabajo más reciente es First Belong to God: On Retreat with Pope Francis (Lo primero es pertenecer a Dios: Un retiro con el Papa Francisco, 2024), basado en los escritos y charlas de Bergoglio como director espiritual de un retiro ignaciano de 8 días. De 2004 a 2006, Ivereigh fue colaborador del entonces arzobispo de Westminster, cardenal Cormac Murphy-O’Connor, uno de los más activos promotores de la candidatura de Jorge Mario Bergoglio al papado. Ivereigh considera que el papado de Francisco inició un giro latinoamericano hacia una iglesia misionera y sinodal, cuyo primer paso fue la exhortación apostólica Evangelii Gaudium (noviembre de 2013), sobre “el anuncio del Evangelio en el mundo actual”, con la cual, dice, “Francisco inaugura una hoja de ruta de su Papado que también es la del pontificado de León”. Pero esa hoja de ruta tenía una génesis anterior: el ya famoso documento de Aparecida, la V Conferencia General del Episcopado Latinoamericano y del Caribe (Celam), redactado por Bergoglio. De esta manera, “América Latina pasó a ser la iglesia fuente”, señala, porque “siempre hay una parte de la Iglesia de la cual brota un dinamismo teológico”. Antes, ese rol lo cumplía Europa, pero a partir del Concilio Vaticano II eso cambia porque es en América Latina donde mejor se lo pone en práctica. Aclara que “fuente” no quiere decir centro; de hecho, “Francisco quería una Iglesia multipolar”. — ¿Hasta qué punto Aparecida refleja a Bergoglio como individualidad y hasta dónde es la Iglesia latinoamericana, que usted define como “fuente”? — El proceso de preparación de esa conferencia general, fue muy sinodal, de mucha consulta, y el papel de Bergoglio en esa conferencia general es muy conocido. Creo que influyó la recepción del Concilio Vaticano II en el Río de La Plata, que tuvo un matiz distinto al resto de América Latina. Tal vez, cuando llegó a Aparecida esa visión sobre la religiosidad popular estaba ya madura. Es decir, una teología de espiritualidad latinoamericana, distinta a anteriores teologías latinoamericanas. Bergoglio tenía muchas cosas que eran de él. Pero también llevaba en su forma de ser y de pensar muchos aportes de la iglesia argentina, la influencia de Lucio Gera y de Rafael Tello y toda esa tradición. — ¿Cómo vio el impacto de su papado en la Argentina? — Creo que una de las razones por las que no vino, sobre todo al principio, fue que tenía horror del triunfalismo. Y sabía que tal vez los argentinos tenían —todos los países lo tienen— una cierta tentación de decir: “El Papa es argentino”. title: Pedro Páez y las fuentes del Nilo Azul
summary: Había sobrevivido a casi siete años de cautiverio en Arabia, aprendido varias lenguas, conocido el café y ganado la confianza de dos negus. Participó en construcciones eclesiásticas y palaciegas y esc
content: Había sobrevivido a casi siete años de cautiverio en Arabia, aprendido varias lenguas, conocido el café y ganado la confianza de dos negus. Participó en construcciones eclesiásticas y palaciegas y escribió una extraordinaria historia de aquel reino africano. Su vida parece un relato de aventuras. Pero tal vez su mayor hazaña no fue encontrar el nacimiento de un río, sino tratar de comprender un país. Dos ojos de agua Gojjam (Etiopía), 21 de abril de 1618. El campamento imperial ha quedado atrás. Pedro Páez avanza por las tierras altas junto a varias personas de la comunidad luso-etíope del séquito del negus Susenyos. Quizá camina fatigado y recuerde las interminables jornadas del desierto de Arabia, cuando su suerte dependía de unos captores a quienes apenas entendía. Sin embargo, ahora conversa con su escolta en un idioma aprendido en África. El paisaje comienza a descender hacia un pequeño valle. Sus acompañantes le señalan dos manantiales: el agua brota limpia en sendas oquedades de apenas cuatro palmos de anchura. Cerca hay huesos de animales sacrificiales. Nada anuncia uno de los grandes enigmas de la geografía clásica. ¿Aquellos modestos hontanares eran realmente el nacimiento del Nilo Azul? Sus guías conocen el lugar, su significado religioso y el curso de las aguas. El viajero introduce una lanza para averiguar la profundidad de las surgencias. En una alcanza el fondo, a unos once palmos. En la otra, no. Anota lo que ha visto y cuanto le refieren. Así pudo desarrollarse aquella jornada: ignoramos qué pensó Páez, pero su presencia en Sakala, el examen de los manantiales y la medición de su hondura con una lanza constan en su Historia de Ethiopia, junto con la alegría que experimentó al verlos. Aquel hombre, nacido cincuenta y cuatro años antes en una pequeña localidad alcarreña, había alcanzado las fuentes del Nilo Azul poco más de siglo y medio antes que James Bruce de Kinnaird. La visita de este escocés en 1770 y su libro Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile le proporcionaron una celebridad que eclipsó durante mucho tiempo al misionero. Tampoco fue el primer visitante de ascendencia europea: João Gabriel, jefe militar de la comunidad luso-etíope, había llegado antes, al parecer durante el reinado de Särsä Dengel (1563-1597), y la noticia circulaba ya en 1607. El mérito de Páez radicó en ofrecer la primera descripción europea extensa y fiable de unos veneros bien conocidos por los naturales. Sin duda, dar con las fuentes del Nilo Azul fue algo inesperado. Había ido a Etiopía para lograr que la Iglesia cristiana de aquel reino reconociera la autoridad papal. La geografía se cruzó en su camino casi por azar. Para comprender cómo llegó hasta allí debemos retroceder unas cuantas décadas. El reino que no estaba donde debía Pedro Páez Jaramillo nació en 1564 en Olmeda de la Cebolla, hoy Olmeda de las Fuentes, en el seno de una familia de la pequeña nobleza castellana. Apenas conocemos su infancia. Pudo iniciar sus estudios superiores en Alcalá de Henares y completó su formación filosófica en el colegio de Belmonte (Cuenca), donde fue discípulo del teólogo navarro Tomás de Ituren. El 18 de junio de 1584 ingresó en la Compañía de Jesús, en el noviciado de Villarejo de Fuentes. Esta orden, fundada en 1534, había convertido las misiones ultramarinas en uno de sus grandes empeños. Sus religiosos predicaban en América, India, China y Japón. El joven quería participar en aquella expansión y el 8 de mayo de 1587 solicitó a sus superiores ser enviado a las Indias. Su petición fue atendida. En abril de 1588 embarcó en Lisboa y meses después llegó a Goa, capital de la India portuguesa (desde 1580 los territorios españoles y portugueses estaban unificados bajo el reinado de Felipe II). En Goa, Páez inició sus estudios teológicos y pronto recibió una misión excepcional: viajar a Etiopía. title: Sharing your faith : practical tips for evangelism
summary: Sharing your faith, or evangelising, is not always an easy experience. For those of us who are not naturally extroverted or confident in public speaking, talking about our faith with people close to u
content: Sharing your faith, or evangelising, is not always an easy experience. For those of us who are not naturally extroverted or confident in public speaking, talking about our faith with people close to us, let alone complete strangers, can be nerve-wracking. Nonetheless, sharing the gospel is something all Christians have been called to participate in through the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20), regardless of our personality, intellectual knowledge or position within the church. As someone who regularly participates in street evangelism and teaches the Bible to young people, I have learnt a few lessons along the way. Here are some practical tips that may help you grow in confidence and approach evangelism with greater love, wisdom and faith. 1. Prepare yourself spiritually First and foremost, it is important to remember that someone’s spiritual growth or acceptance of Christ is ultimately not within our control. Faith is a gift from God, and it is by His grace that hearts are transformed (Ephesians 2:8-9; John 6:44). Our responsibility is to faithfully share the gospel while humbly entrusting the outcome into His hands (Romans 10:14-15). So, pray. Pray for the people you will encounter, for wisdom in your conversations and for the Holy Spirit to guide you (Colossians 4:3-4; James 1:5; Luke 12:12). Read your Bible regularly, not simply to accumulate knowledge or prepare answers, but to know God more deeply through His Word (2 Timothy 3:16-17; Psalm 119:11). The more His Word dwells in your heart, the more naturally it will flow into your conversations (Colossians 3:16; Matthew 12:34). Above all, learn to rely on the Holy Spirit rather than your own intellect, eloquence or comfort. As Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 3:6, one person plants, another waters, but it is God who gives the growth. 2. People are not as scary as they seem One thing I have learnt through evangelism is that people are often not as intimidating as we imagine. Despite our different backgrounds and beliefs, we are all human beings searching for something, whether that is meaning, love, belonging or purpose. If a friend, colleague or family member comes to you for advice or shares something they are struggling with, this can be a natural opportunity to explain how your faith has helped you through similar experiences. And when approaching strangers, you may be surprised by how open some people are to conversations about faith. Many actually know very little about the Bible beyond what they have encountered through popular culture, the media or secular perspectives. Others may have genuine questions but hesitate to ask them for fear of sounding ignorant or offensive. Rather than assuming someone will be hostile or uninterested, approach them with openness and a willingness to listen. You may discover that they are more curious than you expected. 3. Help people understand why they need Jesus and the Church A common response I encounter is something along the lines of, “If Christianity makes you happy, that's great, but it’s just not for me.” Others may say that they are not religious but respect all religions because they encourage people to do good. These responses offer opportunities to explain that Christianity is not simply about personal happiness, moral improvement or following another set of religious rules. At its heart, the Christian faith is about a relationship with God, founded on His love and truth (John 17:3; 1 John 4:9-10). The gospel is for everyone because we all fall short and need God’s grace (Romans 3:23). Jesus did not come merely to make our lives more comfortable, but to reconcile us to God and give us new life (2 Corinthians 5:18-19; John 10:10). Some people may argue that life has no ultimate meaning and that they do not need one to live. Yet even this outlook often involves living according to certain values, purposes or convictions. content: La caída del Imperio romano anuncia la debacle de Europa y la llegada del islam Jesús Córdoba*.- Soy un observador de los acontecimientos de la historia y los comparo fácilmente con lo que pasa en la actualidad. La historia es una disciplina para la que hay que tener un don especial para saber trasmitirla en pocas palabras y sin doblez. Voy a intentar explicarla de la manera más entendible. Quiero enfocarlo todo desde la fe. Porque desde la fe, Roma se salvó, contemplando a los cristianos que ellos mismos asesinaban en sus crueles espectáculos. Observaban con sorpresa que aquellos hombres y mujeres no tenían miedo cuando iban a la muerte, ya que salían cantando y rezando. Se preguntaban loa romanos qué era lo que hacía que no tuviesen miedo, quién era ese Dios que les daba la fortaleza y tranquilidad mientras ellos gemían lastimosamente por la llegada de los barbaros. ¿Cuáles fueron las causas de la caída del Imperio Romano? ¿No son las mismas que sufre ahora la decadente Europa y España dentro de ella? La caída del Imperio Romano fue un proceso largo, por lo que podemos rastrear las causas de su derrumbe siglos atrás, siendo por ello muy importante enumerar todas las razones que conllevaron el final de esta gran civilización. En mi humilde opinión, las causas de la caída del Imperio Romano de Occidente fueron las siguientes: La corrupción en Roma, que era cada vez mayor, y llegaron a un punto que a los mismos senadores les daba igual que sus decisiones fueran malas o buenas para el Imperio, siempre y cuando se pudiesen beneficiar. Hoy, en Europa pasa más o menos lo mismo con la corrupción económica y política. En la moral, el aborto, la destrucción de la familia monogámica formada por hombre y mujer, la perversión de la enseñanza con la ideología de género, la corrupción en la medicina con la eutanasia, la pseudo-ciencia que esclaviza al hombre, la inteligencia artificial que lo anula. Luego, como medida para controlar a los pueblos bárbaros, que presionaban sus fronteras, los romanos tuvieron la idea de unirlos a sus ejércitos, para con ello tener mayor facilidad en neutralizar el peligro que representaban, pero esto también provocaba que los enemigos de Roma comenzaran a ser cada vez más numerosos en el propio ejército imperial. Ahora España y Europa, firman convenios con determinadas naciones para contener la emigración a cambio de grandes cantidades de dinero e inversiones en infraestructuras, agricultura y armamento. Eliminan la agricultura y la industria locales, destruyendo los pantanos de la Península y acogiendo indiscriminadamente a miles de inmigrantes, a los que no hay más remedio que subsidiar, mientras los españoles están en dificultades económicas -muchos en paro-, en los comedores sociales y pidiendo al banco de alimentos. La inflación en Roma era muy alta en su época de mayor decadencia, con enormes impuestos y una población que no podía casi ni comer. La moneda romana estaba tan devaluada que algunos pueblos comenzaron a negociar mediante el trueque. En la actualidad, está cada vez peor el poder adquisitivo. Muchos países europeos tienen una inflación galopante, mientras los gobiernos se llenan de parásitos, chupando de los impuestos abusivos que ponen al pueblo en la precariedad, creando así una bolsa de pobreza alarmante, cargándose la industria, la agricultura y, sobre todo, la unidad de las familias y las personas. El emperador romano perdió poder progresivamente, ya que con los años se deterioró su autoridad centralizadora. Hoy nuestros presidentes, tanto de España como de la Comunidad Europea, han vendido las naciones a un poder demoniaco que está a la sombra y que lleva la Agenda 2030. Agenda que el mismo Papa Francisco promueve y el cardenal Juan José Omeya ha impuesto a toda la Iglesia Española. Quieren destruir a unidad en torno a Jesucristo, creando una nueva religión. On y présente en effet pour la première fois au public le gigantesque Baldaquin de bronze commandé neuf ans plus tôt par le pape Urbain VIII à Gian Lorenzo Bernini, dit Le Bernin. Dans la matinée, les barrières et les échafaudages qui masquent la structure, sous la coupole, sont retirés. La structure est massive, unique en son genre. La foule accourt alors. content: Le christianisme mondial change, peu à peu, de visage. D’ici à 2070, le nombre de chrétiens dans le monde pourrait approcher les 3 milliards, contre 2,27 milliards en 2020.  Une progression de 30% qui devrait être particulièrement spectaculaire en Afrique subsaharienne, où le nombre de chrétiens pourrait bondir de 129% en cinquante ans. Publiées le mercredi 18 novembre, les nouvelles projections du Pew Research Center dessinent ainsi une géographie religieuse en pleine évolution, dans laquelle le continent africain prendra une place toujours plus importante. Le christianisme devrait conserver sa place de première religion mondiale jusqu’en 2035, avant d’être dépassé par l’islam en nombre de fidèles. Selon le Pew Research Center, la population musulmane devrait ainsi augmenter de 80% entre 2020 et 2070, contre 30% pour la population chrétienne. Cette différence de rythme ne signifie toutefois pas que le christianisme recule. Au contraire, ses fidèles devraient être près de 700 millions supplémentaires à l’échelle mondiale d’ici à cinquante ans. title: Ce que l’IA nous fait gagner, ce que le travail nous fait devenir
summary: On entend chaque jour que l’intelligence artificielle va remplacer notre travail. On entend beaucoup moins parler de ce que nous cherchons vraiment à travers notre travail. summary_zh: 我们每天都听到人工智能将取代我们工作的说法。但我们很少听到人们谈论我们通过工作真正想要的是什么。一位从管理人员转变为工匠的人士在《回声报》上的发言提醒我们：在职业活动中，最重要的是什么？实现自我。在迪卡侬工作了十年，其中五年担任一家拥有四十名员工的门店的负责人，35 岁的马蒂厄（Mathieu）辞去了一份高薪的正式工作。
title_zh: 人工智能让我们收获什么，工作让我们成为什么样的人
content: On entend chaque jour que l’intelligence artificielle va remplacer notre travail. On entend beaucoup moins parler de ce que nous cherchons vraiment à travers notre travail. Par son témoignage dans Les Échos, un cadre devenu artisan le rappelle : ce qui compte d’abord dans une activité professionnelle ? Nous accomplir. Après dix années chez Decathlon dont cinq à la tête d’un magasin de quarante personnes, Mathieu quitte à 35 ans un CDI bien rémunéré. Il aimait pourtant le business, l’organisation, la gestion. Mais les horaires, le rythme et le management d’équipe l’ont usé, au point d’aller travailler « la boule au ventre ». Volte-face. Ce qu’il voulait ? Un métier où s’épanouir « à 100% », et non plus à 60 ou 70%. title: From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey
summary: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University, his books, and his journalism for God Reports, ASSIST News Service, and other media […]  The post  From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Brian Nixon Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University , his books, and his journalism for God Reports , ASSIST News Service , and other media outlets. His voice has also reached listeners across the country through his former involvement with the radio program To Every Man an Answer (later known as Pastors’ Perspective ) and, more recently, Paratus , a program devoted to developing a biblical worldview. What may surprise those familiar with Nixon’s academic and journalistic work is that he is also an accomplished musician and songwriter whose musical journey spans more than 30 years. In his forthcoming book, A Beautiful Defense: How Aesthetics Points to God , co-written with Dr. Patrick Zukeran and scheduled for release in 2027 , Nixon explores the relationship between beauty, faith, and the creative process. In anticipation of the book’s release, I spoke with Nixon about his musical beginnings, his creative influences, and his unexpected venture into German electronic music. Tell me about your early musical journey. I grew up in a musical family. Music was part of my everyday life. During high school, I formed a band with some friends that eventually signed with an independent record label in the San Francisco Bay Area. We released only one record, but several of the other members went on to successful careers in the music industry. One became involved in founding Stones Throw Records, an influential independent label known for its underground hip-hop and experimental music. It was an exciting time. We were young, creative, and discovering what music could be. What did you do after the band broke up? I continued my college education, eventually transferring to California State University, Stanislaus. There, I met another group of musicians, and we formed a band called Canterbury. We ended up winning a Bay Area battle-of-the-bands competition, which was exciting. But rather than continuing in that direction, we decided to pursue something with a more intentional ministry focus. That led to the formation of Widow’s Mite . Widow’s Mite eventually signed with Rick Wakeman, the legendary keyboardist of Yes. Interestingly, that connection also introduced me to journalist Dan Wooding, who wrote Wakeman’s first biography. That relationship eventually opened the door for me to write for ASSIST News Service . So, in a rather unexpected way, my musical career helped launch my journalism career. Widow’s Mite After college, did you continue writing music? Absolutely. I still write music today. My compositions range from jazz and pop to what I call tone poems —short instrumental works that emphasize mood, atmosphere, and musical expression. Some are experimental, while others are much more accessible. I’ve always enjoyed exploring different musical forms rather than staying within a single genre. Interestingly, some of my recent compositions have been selected for rotation by a German online radio station. And here’s the surprising part: they’re German electronic and techno-influenced songs. I’ve been experimenting with AI-assisted production, including using a synthesized female vocalist to interpret my compositions. Did you say German techno? (Laughs.) I know. It sounds funny, doesn’t it? But there’s a story behind it. Recently, I took a deep dive into the music of Kraftwerk, the pioneering German electronic band. I was familiar with their work during high school in the early 1980s because they had influenced so many of the post-punk bands I was listening to at the time. I decided to revisit their entire catalog, and I was blown away all over again. They were years ahead of their time. Their approach to rhythm, synthesizers, repetition, and technology helped shape entire genres of contemporary music.

content: By Charles Gardner — Charles and Linda on their wedding day My wife Linda had no idea of the Jewish background of her employers during the 1970s and 80s. She just knew that she loved working for them and only left to follow God’s call to work with children. So we travelled down to London for an exhibition of the Salmon and Gluckstein dynasty, and the story of how these resilient Jewish families fled violent persecution in Eastern Europe to build what became the largest catering company in the world known as J Lyons & Co. Linda worked there as a home economist from 1977-1984 but it was only much later that she learnt of the Jewish nature of the firm that once literally fed Britain with its teashops and corner houses on every high street, and its products in every home, Linda playing her part through her cooking and marketing skills. A few years later, after graduating from Bible College in Bournemouth, she worked at a prayer and reconciliation centre in Northern Ireland where she was introduced to the importance of the Christian faith’s Jewish roots, as a result of which she took a study tour of Israel to learn more. And on a second trip to the Holy Land ten years later, she got more than she bargained for. At Cana in Galilee, where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, Linda was given a vision of her own wedding. And we met on a blind date six months later! Though having Jewish ancestry myself, I grew up knowing nothing about it. But I learnt more later, especially after becoming a Christian in my early twenties, as Linda had done. It helped that I had a Jewish believer as my early mentor, and I became increasingly aware of the significance of our Jewish heritage, about which I now write prolifically. Meanwhile Linda, who has been teaching Christianity in Doncaster area schools for over 30 years, also now teaches about Judaism as it forms the context into which Christ came to us, fulfilling all the laws and promises of the Old Testament. So in both our cases, we were kept in the dark about very important aspects of our lives – until the Lord shone his light on the truth. Which brings me to the Christian Church as a whole, especially in the UK. We have known very little, if anything, of our faith’s Jewish roots or of God’s ongoing purposes for Israel. This needs to change – and fast! For we are surely hurtling towards the Messiah’s Second Coming like a high-speed train, in danger of coming off the rails with the rest of humanity if we fail to get to grips with how we Christians fit into the unfolding picture of global opposition to tiny Israel. What is our role as we watch antisemitism spread across the globe like wildfire? Do we just sit and watch, or write it off as having nothing to do with us, and remain silent? Or do we stand up to be counted as those who refuse to salute the new Nazism that portrays itself as anti-Zionism – a Confessing Church walking the way of the cross for God’s chosen people? My questions come as renewed calls are made for an independent inquiry into antisemitism at the BBC following news that Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon has won £400,000 in compensation from the broadcaster. Lucie’s career is said to have unravelled after she raised concerns about antisemitism within the BBC, though the latter have not admitted to any fault. This is highly significant as millions of UK Christians are (where Israel is concerned) probably more influenced by what they hear from our national broadcaster than what they read in the Bible. title: New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran
summary: By Howard Cooper — Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the […]  The post  New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Howard Cooper — Abdul Al-Sayed (wikipedia commons) Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the Senate and the first epidemiologist to serve in the chamber, according to WION News. In an interview with NPR’s Leila Fadel, he said, “I will likely swear on a Quran. Which Quran, we’re not sure.” He pointed to a copy once owned by Thomas Jefferson, which Keith Ellison used when he was sworn in to Congress, and to an old Quran at the University of Michigan that he described as the first in the state. The US Constitution does not require a Bible or any religious text. In practice, senators usually take the formal oath together on the Senate floor, and a Bible comes into play in individual ceremonial swearings-in. El-Sayed hasn’t said whether he’ll use the Quran in the formal proceedings, the ceremony, or both, and that his choice would not alter the wording of the oath. He has also stressed that his oath will be to the U.S. Constitution,  according to IBTimes. He will be sworn in by Vice President JD Vance, a fact El-Sayed has noted with humor. The Blaze reported he called it a “delicious irony” that Vance is constitutionally required to do so. Not everyone is comfortable with the news. The Daily Signal reported that former White House press secretary Sean Spicer said this week that given El-Sayed’s connections and statements, he should undergo a formal background check before receiving classified information. Presumably, Spicer was referring to Al-Sayed’s family connections to the Muslim Brotherhood. For many Christians, the moment raises questions about the role of faith in public life, the long American tradition of religious liberty, and the Judeo-Christian roots of the United States. El-Sayed and his colleagues are scheduled to be sworn in at noon on January 3, 2027. The post New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran first appeared on God Reports .

summary: By Charles Gardner — A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there. Luai Ahmed was invited to […]  The post  Yemeni journalist visits Israel, dramatically changes views  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Charles Gardner — Luai Ahmed speaking at UN (screenshot YouTube) A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there. And he was led to the conclusion that everything he has been taught to believe about the Jews is a lie. Luai Ahmed was invited to address the assembly by UN Watch, a non-governmental organisation monitoring the international body’s performance, as the UN Human Rights Council gathered to debate racism. He said: “I grew up in Yemen, where the word that we used for black people is ‘abeed’, which quite literally means ‘slaves’. Racism towards black people in my country is horrifying, but it’s not even the most toxic hatred that I was taught. “The first time I ever heard the word ‘Jew’ was in my local mosque when I was nine years old. At the end of Friday prayers, the Imam said: ‘May Allah kill the Jews and the Zionists’. And I responded alongside thousands of Muslims praying beside me: ‘Ameen’.” Luai then continued: “I was taught that Zionism meant killing Arabs, stealing our land, and destroying Islam. Then October 7th came. Hamas terrorists ‘freed Palestine’ by slaughtering 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping more than 200 people, including a one-year-old child. “Almost everyone in my Arab-Muslim circle celebrated. I didn’t. Instead, as a journalist, I decided to visit the so-called Zionist entity, and I was completely shocked to the core by the lack of apartheid and racism that I experienced. “One day, I got an eye infection. At the hospital, the nurses in reception were Jewish. The doctor treating me was Arab. Is there racism in Israel? Of course. There’s racism everywhere. “But Arabs in Israel aren’t called ‘slaves’. They are doctors, engineers, and party leaders. My experience helped me realise that Zionism really just means the Jewish people’s right to a tiny country. Everything I was taught was a lie.” Quite apart from tipping over the tables of woke left-wing ideology spreading its poisonous antisemitic tentacles across the globe, Luai’s testimony also knocks holes into the escalating pressure on the UK to make reparations for the slave trade, which saw plenty of collaborators in the host countries of those who suffered. And of course, the truth that dare not speak its name – that it was Christians like William Wilberforce who put an end to it! Luai is a great inspiration to fellow journalists like me who long for more of our colleagues to stand up and be counted. Thanks also to David Soakell of Christian Friends of Israel’s Watching Over Zion newsletter, November 5, 2026. title: Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin
summary: By Mark Ellis — Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, […]  The post  Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Amber Sparks (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, especially with the Rigs-to-Reefs program, when oil drilling platforms are decommissioned. “We work with the oil companies to repurpose certain parts of the platform, retrofit it so that it can remain in place and continue to function as an artificial reef,” she told God Reports. Amber’s work has taken her around the world, with many dive experiences and encounters in the ocean with marine life. But there is one story she will never forget. It happened in the Gulf of Mexico shortly after Amber graduated from Scripps Institute and was invited on a research industry cruise with oil company representatives, scientists, and regulators on a liveaboard vessel. At the Flower Garden National Banks, a marine protected area 200 miles offshore, Amber was excited about her first dive, but slightly nervous. “You don’t know what you’re going to see or what this experience is going to be like,” she recalls. Dropping in (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook) Each diver had to jump off the vessel to get in the water. “We’re all geared up with our snorkel, our buoyancy control device, our wetsuit, and fins are the last thing you put on. So, I put on my fins and I jumped off the side of the boat.” “The second that I hit the water, one of my fins fell off, and I looked down and watched as it slowly descended to the bottom.” Amber glanced over at her dive buddy, and said, “I’m gonna go down. I’m going down.” Normally she would wait for her dive partner and they would go down together, but in this case, she thought, “I can’t (wait). I gotta go get my fin.” So Amber slowly began to descend to the bottom, about 60 feet below the ocean surface. “I felt completely lost. I was in a completely new area. I never dove before, and now I only had one fin.” She realized there were major currents that could have moved her fin in any direction. “I realized I can’t really swim with just one fin. So now not only am I at depth, but I’m handicapped with just one fin, and I started to feel pretty nervous.” It would probably take her 10 minutes to get back the surface, with safety stops. At the moment before panic set in, she looked upward and saw an amazing sight. It was a giant manta ray, with wings extending at least 10 feet. “Its wingspan was double mine. Its arms were out, and it was coming up over the side of a reef. “I’ve never seen a manta ray like this before. It totally took my breath away, it was so magnificent.” Another manta ray (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) She noted that manta rays are known in the ocean community to be “majestic, God-connected creatures with an understanding maybe beyond what humans can fully comprehend. They see the world and feel it in another way,” she notes. Mantas have the largest known brain of any fish. Their brains are large in absolute terms and relative to body size, which is also true of elephants, dolphins, and people. Their brains have enlarged areas associated with intelligence, vision, and motor coordination, and some of their brain cells are more like those in birds and mammals than in other fish.(1) As the manta ray drew close to Amber, she had an unusual communication experience. “I felt this sense where it said, ‘I want you to follow me. I’m going to help you find your fin.’ Amber Sparks Amber’s diving partner had just descended next to her, and they both began to swim after the manta. “I was barely making it, following this manta ray across the reef. At this point, I was so excited to see a manta ray. I kind of forgot about being handicapped, and I was just trying to go as fast as I can to keep up with it. Then Amber got the sur

content: The word epiphany is defined by the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary as “a sudden and surprising moment of understanding.” Often, such epiphany moments arrive unexpectedly, interrupting the ordinary rhythms of life with extraordinary insight. Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Eliott Davis Sitting beneath artist James Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany on the campus of Rice University in Houston, Texas, on a Sunday morning as the sun rose, the word epiphany took on new meaning. As the morning light slowly illuminated the sky, subtle shifts in color transformed the space above me. The experience was both architectural and atmospheric, a convergence of art, nature, and contemplation. Turrell, born in 1943, is an American artist internationally recognized for his exploration of light, space, and human perception. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Turrell’s artistic vision reflects an appreciation for silence, stillness, and inward reflection. Commissioned by Rice University through the generosity of alumna Suzanne Deal Booth, Twilight Epiphany opened in 2012 as part of the university’s public art program. The pyramidal Skyspace, designed to accommodate approximately 120 visitors, features an aperture in its roof through which viewers observe the changing sky. At sunrise and sunset, carefully programmed LED lights interact with the natural atmosphere, creating an extraordinary experience of shifting color and perception. More than a work of architecture, the installation invites visitors to slow down, look upward, and reconsider the relationship between light and the world around them. James Turrell (Chat GPT) For me, the experience was something of a spiritual exercise. Light, after all, is among the Bible’s most enduring metaphors for divine revelation, truth, and beauty. As the colors shifted above me, I was reminded that beauty does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it simply asks us to be still and pay attention. Rothko Chapel. Photo: https://www.mark-rothko.org/rothko-chapel.jsp#google_vignette. From Rice University, I headed to another meditative landmark: the Rothko Chapel . Here, I sat among the monumental, dark-hued paintings of Mark Rothko, contemplating both the tragedy of the artist’s life and the triumph of the chapel that bears his name. Commissioned by Houston philanthropists John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and dedicated in 1971, the Rothko Chapel is an interfaith sanctuary devoted to contemplation, spiritual reflection, and human rights. Its octagonal interior contains fourteen large-scale paintings by Rothko, whose subtle variations of black, maroon, and purple create an atmosphere of profound stillness. Rothko, born Marcus Rothkowitz in 1903, was a leading figure in American Abstract Expressionism, celebrated for his ability to evoke deep emotional responses through color and form. Yet his personal life was marked by physical illness, depression, and emotional turmoil. In February 1970, before the chapel’s dedication, Rothko died by suicide at the age of sixty-six. He never witnessed the completed sanctuary that would become one of his most enduring artistic legacies. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Brian C. Nixon There is something deeply moving about this juxtaposition. An artist whose life ended in despair left behind a place where countless visitors have sought peace, meaning, and solace. The darkness of Rothko’s paintings does not necessarily communicate hopelessness. Rather, their quiet intensity invites viewers to confront the depths of human experience—sorrow, longing, mystery, and perhaps even transcendence. Where Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany draws the eyes upward toward the heavens, Rothko’s chapel seems to draw the gaze inward, toward the mysteries of the human soul. title: Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success
summary: While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence […]  The post  Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: John Warwick Montgomery While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence with C. S. Lewis and his barrister gowns to the thousands of books that comprise his remarkable personal collection, Lanier has provided the Christian world with a marvelous tribute to one of the great Christian intellectuals of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Born in 1931, John Warwick Montgomery (d. 2024) was a distinguished Christian apologist, theologian, attorney, and scholar whose extraordinary career spanned several disciplines. Holding numerous academic degrees, including doctorates in theology, philosophy, and law, Montgomery became internationally recognized for his defense of Christianity through historical evidence, legal reasoning, and philosophical argumentation. His influential books, including History and Christianity , Faith Founded on Fact , and The Shape of the Past , helped establish a rigorous approach to Christian apologetics. Whether lecturing in universities, debating skeptics, or practicing law, Montgomery maintained that Christianity was not merely a matter of subjective belief but a faith grounded in historical reality and rational inquiry. Yet to stop at the library would be to understate Lanier’s remarkable work. The sixth annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series was a tour de force of distinguished thinkers, passionate Christians, and intellectually engaging presentations. More than a commemoration of Montgomery’s life, the gathering represented a continuation of his intellectual legacy: the conviction that Christianity can withstand serious scrutiny and offer compelling answers to life’s most profound questions. Mark Lanier, Nancy Pearcey, Paul Gould, Adam Francisco, and Michael Horton From the opening panel discussion hosted by attorney and philanthropist Mark Lanier to Dr. Paul Gould’s thoughtful presentation on worldviews, followed by attorney Craig Parton’s lecture on jurisprudential apologetics, one theme emerged with unmistakable clarity: Christianity is a reasonable faith. The presentations reflected Montgomery’s own interdisciplinary approach to apologetics: the Christian faith and intellectual inquiry need not be adversaries. Indeed, the Christian tradition has long insisted that faith and reason are complementary avenues in the pursuit of truth. The following day continued this rich intellectual exploration. Professor Nancy Pearcey addressed questions surrounding truth, dismantling various modern ideologies, while Dr. Adam Francisco offered an informative overview of Islamic history and belief, helping participants better understand one of world’s biggest religions. The keynote address by Dr. Michael Horton examined the challenge of reaching those who identify as “spiritual but not religious,” a growing segment of contemporary society. Horton’s presentation underscored the importance of communicating historic Christian truth in a culture increasingly suspicious of religious institutions yet often deeply interested in spiritual meaning. Dr. Michael Horton On Sunday morning, Lanier founder, Mark Lanier, hosted many participants during his Biblical literacy class, where he continued the dialogue with Michael Horton. Taken together, the lectures, discussions, and interviews demonstrated the breadth of Christian scholarship and the continuing relevance of thoughtful apologetics in an age of skepticism, religious pluralism, and cultural uncertainty. content: What do Jesus and Isaiah have in common? Quite a bit, according to renowned British New Testament scholar N. T. Wright. Gathering at the marvelous Lanier Theological Library in Houston, Texas—the brainchild of noted attorney, author, and biblical scholar Mark Lanier—Wright offered a packed house in the Great Room a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between the Old Testament prophet Isaiah and the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Dr. Joseph Holden of Veritas International University listening to Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. For Wright, Isaiah is far more than an ancient prophetic voice whose words occasionally appear in the New Testament. Rather, the prophet provides a theological framework for understanding Jesus and the unfolding purposes of God. In his book Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright invites readers to rediscover the extraordinary depth of Isaiah’s prophetic vision, demonstrating how its themes of judgment, restoration, redemption, and new creation find their ultimate expression in Christ. Central to Wright’s interpretation is the conviction that Isaiah’s message cannot be separated from the larger story of Israel. The prophet speaks of exile and homecoming, divine judgment and covenant faithfulness, suffering and salvation. These themes, Wright argues, become essential to understanding how Jesus understood his own mission and how the earliest Christians interpreted his life. Particularly significant is Isaiah’s portrayal of the suffering servant, whose affliction becomes the means through which God’s redemptive purposes are accomplished. Wright connects this prophetic imagery to Jesus’ sacrificial death, while emphasizing that the cross cannot be isolated from the broader biblical promise of God’s restoration of creation. Equally important is Isaiah’s vision of a renewed world, a creation in which justice, righteousness, and peace flourish under God’s reign. For Wright, the resurrection of Jesus announces the beginning of that promised new creation. The Christian hope, therefore, is not simply an escape from the present world, but the ultimate renewal of God’s good creation. Personal Stories: Mounting Up with Wings Like Eagles Amid the theological insights and biblical exposition, Wright shared several personal stories, offering the audience a glimpse into how the words of Isaiah have shaped not only his scholarship but also his spiritual imagination. One story centered on the beloved passage from Isaiah 40:31, in which the prophet declares that those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles. Wright recalled preaching on Isaiah many years earlier and drew an amusing comparison to the long-running British radio program Desert Island Discs , in which notable guests select the recordings they would take with them if stranded on a deserted island. “I’ve sometimes said I have a set of desert island texts,” Wright explained, suggesting that certain biblical passages remain especially meaningful throughout one’s life. Near the top of his list, he said, is the closing portion of Isaiah 40, with its magnificent image of soaring eagles. The passage, he suggested, is more than a favorite theological text. It is part of his personal testimony, a biblical promise that has accompanied him through the years. A second story brought the imagery of Isaiah into an unexpected encounter with the natural world. While completing the final proofreading of Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright and his wife, Maggie, were staying at their home in Scotland. Wright was alone in a room, carefully reviewing the text, when something outside caught his attention. “Out of the corner of my eye, I saw something,” he recalled. “At first, I thought it was somebody’s dog that had come into our front garden.” Noted Biblical archeologist, Dr. Steven Collins, listening to Mark Lanier interview Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library.
